summary: The assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,00,000 as the total wealth of the assessee. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. In appeal before the Tribunal, the High Court held that the assessee was liable to wealth Tax for the relevant assessment years in question and that it had not been shown that accrued interest on accrual basis. On reference, the Tribunal referred the following questions to the High court: (1) Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Wealth Tax officer was in law justified in including in the net wealth of an assessee under the Wealth tax Act; (2) Whether the assessee had been assessed to income tax for a reference of the cases to this Court in view of the conflict of opinion between the Orissa High Court and the Andhra Pradesh High Court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The computation of the net assets of an asses see is to be determined as it obtains on a particular date. [310C] 2. In order that a wealth tax may be included in the wealth of a assessee under section 3 of the Wealth Act, the valuation date for the purposes of this Act shall be the last day of the previous year as defined in the Income tax Act. The method of accounting is mercantile or cash or hybrid, is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets of the asses see. [311D] 3. In the instant case, there was an obvious advantage in adopting as the valuation dates in terms of the last date of the income tax "previous year" taking into account the financial activities of the appellant during that "previous years". The method adopted by the assessee is to he taken into account and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accounting or another. There is clear indication that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounts adopted by him. [312E F] 4. In view of this, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts of the assesses were maintained on cash basis interest due on accrual method, yet there was no reason why the assessee should have been shown as entitled to be included within the assets in the Wealthtax Act. That being so, the finding is inescapable and must be set aside. [313C D] 5. The conclusion is inevitable that even if the accounts were maintained at cash basis, interest due from accrual method of account adopted by assessee would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation day. It is immaterial if the assessee employed one system or another, that there was a change in the position of the business of the respondent during that time. [309F G] 6. The principle of determining assets of a person has to be taken into consideration and it was immaterial whether he employs one method of accountancy or other. There are clear indication in the definition or "net wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value". [310G H] 7. In this view of all the assets, the assessee cannot be said to have been assessed as a "net Wealth" within the meaning of the Act.

The respondent was dismissed from service by the Central Administrative Tribunal. The appellant, a Government servant, filed an appeal before the Central Adminis tration Tribunal which held that the order of dismissal passed by the Tribu nal on a public servant could not be sustained. The Tribunal also held that since the respondent had been given an opportunity to defend himself in the enquiry, he should have been reinstated in service and that the punishment of dismissal should be maintained. The High Court set aside the order and directed reinstatement of the respondent with full back wages. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to pass any orders under section 14(1) of the Act, as the Central Government had no juris diction to direct the Governor to review the penalty, for as the disciplinary authority could not have exercised its powers under section 15(1), the order was bad. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The power conferred on the Central Govern ment by the rules is a judicial power and it is not for the court to consider whether the ground alone would have weigh with the authority in dismissing the public servant. If the High Court is satisfied that there is no sufficient ground for interference with the penalty if the conclusion of the Inquiry Officer or the Tribunal prima facie make out a case of misdemeanour for which the punishment can lawfully be imposed, it is neither for the court to consider any question of misconduct for which he could lawfully be inflicted. [501C D] 2. The Court has no jurisdiction if the findings of the inquiry officer or the Tribun al are based on evidence even if some of them is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. If it is his case that he was not in fact the person convicted, it would have weighed with him in passing the order. [500D] 3. The question whether the penalty of dismissal from service imposed upon the appellant was a matter which could properly be decided by the Tribunal under section 30(1)(c) of . [502E F] 4. The jurisdiction to impose a lesser penalty is not a judicial function and it cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously. It is not open to the Court to sit as a court of appeal over a decision based on it. If there is any error in law apparent on the face of the record, the High Courts would have jurisdiction to exercise all the powers under the Act. [525F G] 5. The order of the Tribunal imposing a lesser punishment on the appellant is not liable to be set aside.

The appellant was the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff. The suit was decreed by the Trial Court and the first appellate court. The second appeal filed by the defendant No. 1 was dismissed as the trial court had no jurisdiction to decide the question whether the suit was barred by Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court held that the plaintiff was not entitled to possession of the property in respect of which he claimed to be a lessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the second suit based on the factum of tenancy was not maintainable as the subsequent suit was hit by section 58(2) of Act No. 2 of 1965 and therefore, the subsequent action taken by the trial Court was barred under Order 2 rule 2(1) of Code of civil Procedure. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the Civil Courts is specifically barred by sub section (2)of Section 58 from settling, deciding or dealing with any question which is by or under the Act required to be settled, decided and dealt with by the Mamlatdar. [802C] 2. It would be just and fair that the issue whether a person is a tenant or a deemed tenant was required to he decided by the Civil Court as incidental to the grant of relief for possession or is the Civil court precluded from deciding the same in view of section 7 read with section 58 (2). [803D] 3. The question which arose in the suit, was whether defendant No 1 proved that he was a tenant in respect thereof. If on the other hand he was held to be tenant, the Civil Judge could decide the said question. In such a situation the remedy may not be the one available in the case of a tenant other than a deemed landlord whose case is not governed by section 8(2). But in the instant case, the civil court would not be competent to pass any order for restoration of possession to the deemed tenant. [903E F] 4. The decision of the Mamlatdar is final and binding on the parties. It will be just as fair that a suit instituted in a Civil Court issues which are required to been settled, decide and dealt With by any authority patent to settle, decide or deal with any questions which are by or Under the Act, the jurisdiction of civil courts to settle or dealwith any question whether such person is or is not required to do so. [1003G H] 5. The expression "any other court" in section 58 of the Act means a Court established under the Code. It does not mean that a court which has no jurisdiction over a suit can decide by itself the question as to who is a landlord and whether he is a deemed purchaser of the land. [1103G] 6. The word "court" in Section 8(1)(a) of Bombay Tenancy Act, 1948 means a court established under section 4 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950. It includes a court within its jurisdiction to settle and deal with the same. [1204C D] 7. The Court is not competent to decide any question as regards the nature of the questions required to determine for grant or refusal of relief claimed in the plaint.

The petitioners are carpenters in the Government service. They are employed as carpenter and they are being paid the same wages as are payable to carpentants, painters and carpentors ' helpers ' aiders. The Government has not fixed the minimum wages for similar work in the construction industry. The petitioners have been treated differently from the other employees of the Corporation. They have been paid the minimum wage prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like posts. Their case is that the unit where the petitioners are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act. The petitioner No. 1 is employed by a company incorporated under the . The Government had not fixed their wages as carpenterers or in the alternative, the minimum pay of the regular employees as carpents and they were being paid them the same rates as are applicable to carpenterants, Painters and unskilled items. They also applied for regularisation of their services as carpanters. Their claim was rejected by the Government on the ground that they had not been paid any wages in terms of the contract of employment or otherwise. The State Government has filed this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the constitutional validity of the Act and the constitutional vires of the provisions of the . Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The principle of "equal pay for equal work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by Article 14 of the Constitu tion. It is true that the petitioners are employed by the company incorporated in the FactoriesAct and by the general description of their job, one cannot come to the conclusion that every carpenter or craftsmen is equal to the other in the performance of his work. The principal claim of the petitioners therefore fails and is rejected. [667B C] 1.2 The principle has to be read into Article 14 which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before law or the equal protection of the law and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. [668D] 1:3 The principle is applicable only to skilled and unskilled workers in Government service, but not to skilled or unskilled workmen. It has not been extended to employees of a Corporation. The Court, therefore, cannot direct the Corporation to apply the rates prescribed under exhibit P.

The appellants were charged with the offence of murder of one Malan and his wife, accused 1 and 2. The prosecution case was that on the day of occurrence the deceased and his father were seen together at about 4 p.m. in the morning of October 1975 at about 7 p.M. and when they reached the house of the deceased, the deceased came to the house and saw the deceased lying dead. On the night of October, 1975, the accused 1, 6 and 7 were sleeping near the house. The deceased was seen by PW 2 and his mother in law and PW 3. The accused 1 was also found guilty under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. for having committed the murder of Malan. The High Court acquitted all the accused except accused 1. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the retracted judicial confession of accused 1 to 4 could not be relied upon against them in view of the fact that they were not parties to the conspiracy and in furtherance of their common intention they committed the offence under section 34 read with Section 34 I P.C., and (2) the High Court had no jurisdiction to convict the appellants for the offence punishable under section 304B I. P. C. because the retracted Judicial confession was not admissible in evidence against them. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confessions of accused 5 and 6 are admissible in law. [695G] 2.1 The retracted confession of the accused 5 is admissible in terms of section 34 of the Evidence Act. It is true that the retracted confession is not admissible under section 32 of the Indian Evidence Act but it is admissible under sec.34 I.p.C.[696A B] 2:2 In the instant case, the retracted confessional statement of accused No. 1 and 6 was recorded by the Magistrate on a consideration of the evidence and all the four accused were acquitted by the High court. [797B C] 3.1 It is well settled that the confession of an accused person is admissible as a whole and it is not necessary for the Court to examine the maker of the statement under section 27 or section 34, I.PC. [896C D] 2 :3 The retracted Judicial confessions of the two accused are inadmissible in evidence. The confession of one of the four persons who had been tried along with other accused 1 is admissible. [997D] 3:2 It is not open to the Court under section 439 Cr. P C. to convict an accused for the murder and to convict him for the same offence. The court has no power to convict a person for the offences of murder and it can be used only in cases where there are other circumstances which make out a case against him. [1097E F] 3 :3 In the present case, there is no evidence that the accused 6 was not a party to charge No.4 which was framed only against them under section 120B I P C., and no appeal against their acquittal had been filed in the High Courts. The conviction of the appellant under section 307 read with 34 IP. C., could be sustained. [1197F G] 4:1. In view of this fact that accused 6 and7 were not a parties to charge Nos.4, 5 and 7, they were acquitted. [1299G] 3 2:3 The High Courts have no jurisdiction under section 423 Cr.P C., to convict them for the offenses of murder. [1397F] 4.2. In the absence of any evidence that accused 1 had been convicted or acquitted by a Court of law, it is open to him to take into consideration all the circumstances which show that he was not guilty of the offence charged.

The appellant was the sole executor of the will executed by his father in favour of his father. The testator died leaving behind two sons, one son and another son. The appellant 's father died in 1945. The will was registered as a will in respect of the properties of the deceased. The question for determination was whether the will was proved to be the last will and testament of the testator. Held, that the High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that it was not shown that the testator had signed the will at the relevant time when he attested the will. The evidence of the appellant as well as the attesting witness showed that the will had been executed by the testator on August 22, 1945 and that the signature of the scribe was not proved. The High Court had rightly held that the appellant had not established that the execution of the document was not duly proved. Held further, that it could not be said that the propounder would have known the contents of the Will at the time when she signed the instrument. The onus to prove that the executant fully understood the contents and dispositions in the will is on him. The burden of proving that the attesting witnesses were not present at the place of the writing was very heavy, and it was always of great importance in this case. Held also, further, the High court was in wrong in coming into the conclusion, that there was no evidence to show that the testatrix fully understood its contents. The signature of a testator on the will raised a presumption that the document had been signed by the executant before he put his signatures to the document and it is always of very great importance that the genuineness of the signature must be proved beyond doubt.

The appellant company was registered as "Cinema Arcons" under the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The sales tax authorities levied sales tax on these goods and assessed them to sales tax for two assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 77 on the ground that they fell under entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Andhra State General Sales tax Act,1957. The appellant company challenged the validity of the said assessments on the grounds (1) that the sales tax was not leviable as it was not "agricultural machinery" within the meaning of Entry 41 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution; (2) that they fall under entry 41 of the State List in which they occur, and (3) that their turnover exceeded the limit prescribed by the entry in the 1 st Schedule. The High Court held that the goods fell under Entry 41 and not under consideration. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the Sales Tax Authorities were entitled to raise an objection that they were covered by the 4th entry in respect of items which are so very different and could have only a very remote hearing, if any, upon any reasoning which could be adopted to support the submission that the are carbons under consideration; (4) that in both these cases what was decided was whether "cinema" was covered by Entry 41. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word "electrical goods" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. It will be noticed that the entry is a residuary one and cannot be read into it merely because a purchaser makes some other use of it. [562 B] 2. The words "required for use there with" have been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. The fact that they can also be used for search lights, signalling, stage lighting, or where strong light is used for building purposes would not cease to be covered by an entry meant for goods sold for agricultural purposes merely because some of them are also sold to agriculturists for agricultural pur poses. [563 E] 3. The expression "requirement for use" in the Schedule to include parts". It will, therefore, be clear that the word "attached" is employed in the schedules to describe articles which may be manufactured for purposes of business. [564 B C] 4. The term "parts thereof" is not used in any sense as well as in any other kind of instrument of gadget only, the article, manufactured to serve as a part of a particular kind of apparatus, would not lose its character as covered by that entry merely because the purchaser makes certain other use. [565 E] 5. The definition of "electricity" is given in the Explanation to section 2(4) of the Act. It would be noticed from the fact that the words "part ' thereof" are used in various entries, such as entry No., 4 of 1st schedule to the Mysore General Sales (Taxes) Act, 1958. [567 E] 6. The use of the word 'electricity ' is used by reference to goods which might have been purchased for use in a particular type of instrument or gadgets. It may be noticed in the context that they are known as "cins" which are required for use therein. [568 G H] 7. The meaning of this entry cannot be given to the word `electricity". [567 F] 8. The intention of the framers of the schedule in making the entry was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. It is clear from the facts that they have been known as 'cinissa ' in the market. This finding was enough, in the absence of any evidence which could he adopted to justify the view taken by the Andhra praes sioner.

The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of a notification issued by the State Government under section 15 of the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966, on the ground that it was violative of Article 304(b) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the impugned notification was in contravention of clause (b) and (c) of article 304(a) of Constitution. In these petitions it was contended for the petitioners that under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution, the royalty recovered by the Government had to be used only for mineral development and could not be used for any other purpose. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The State Government is empowered to make rules for regulating the grant of quarry leases or other minerals in respect of minor minerals. Under clause (a) the holder of a mining lease or any other mineral concession granted under any rule made under sub section (1) shall pay royalty at the rate of 50 per cent of the rate applicable to such lessee and no royalty is payable by village potters who manufacture upto one lakh bricks per year. The petitioners are not entitled to any relief in these writ petitions. [408C D] 2. The impugned notification in question was in violation of clause(b), (c), (d) and(e) of Article 301 of the Constitu tion. Under cl. (a), the State has power to make a classification for purposes of implementing the policy of the Act under which the Rules are made. [416D] 3. The fact that section 15 is passed for devel opment of minerals, but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in the public interest and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said tax should be used merely for mineral Development purposes. [414F] 4. The Act is passed in respect to minor minerals which are being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the state. Under section 15(1) a holder of any mining lease, or any person who manufacture beyond one lakh brick earth or any agent, manager, employee, contractor or sub lessee from the leased area at the rates specified in column 3 of the Schedule to this Act may pay royalty in respect thereof. [413F G] 5. The word "any other mineral concessions" is defined in section 2(g) of that Act as a result of which the State may be granted upto three years, and by the village potterters whose annual production was not exceeding two lakh bricks to the Rural Housing Board or Panchayats. Under sub clause (c). the State Legislature has power under sub cl.(a) to make any classification for purpose of implementing it. [411F G; 414A] 6. The expression "any mining lease shall be granted for an area exceeding 10 hectares in case of specified minor minerals and not for other purpose sanctioned by law. Under el. (b), the holder or a lessee is entitled to quarry lease for an Area exceeding 10 acres in case where specified minor mineral is not less than 10 acres. The clause further provides that no royalty shall be charged from any mine exceeding 10 tons in case the area of which a Parwana could be issued and the duration of the Parwana right and as also the period of the lease, if any, shall be paid by village or land covered by a mining leases. [420C D; 414D] 7. The term "any mine" has to be read in its ordinary sense and not in its popular sense. The words "any mines" have been defined in cl. 2(h) of section 2 of the . The fact, that section 5 of the , does no doubt make any distinction between a mining lessee or any mine which is being treated by him as part and for other matters sanctioned by the law. [409D E] 8.

The appellant was the founder of a temple. The trusteeship of the temple was "hereditary" and the appellant was appointed as the trustee of the Math. The appellant 's father died in 1960 leaving behind his widow, his wife and children. The respondents filed a suit for declaration that the appellant is a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree on the ground that the succession was "regulated by usage" and therefore the suit should be dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The right of the trustees to appoint is vested in the assembly of a religious institution. The right to appoint must be vested in an office of hereditary trustee. [434 B] (2) The succession to the office of a hereditary Trustee is in the nature of property. It is not the case of the appellant that the trustees of the institution are hereditary trustees because their office ' devolves by hereditary right or because succession to that office is specifically provided for by the founder. In the present case, the custom in (1 ) (2), which was adopted by the appellant, was not a hereditary one within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Act. [427 B C] (3) The word "succession" in section 6 (9) is used in two different senses and it is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the death of an existing mahant, his chela does not succeed to the post as a matter of course.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted him of the charge under section 307 IPC and awarded sentence to him for life. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the evidence of PW 4 in so far as he implicated the second accused was not corroborated by medical evidence; (ii) the testimony of PW4 in so much as he was not examined as an absconder; and (iii) the High Court erred in convicting the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The conviction of the appel lant is set aside and the accused is acquitted. [707E] 2. The evidence of the sole eye witness has been rejected with reference to the first information report only because he was a witness. He had stated in the first Information Report that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accusedelasan alias Appa Rao, who was a leper, and that he had not seen the assailants who might have escaped. The fact that the eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased brother as early as possible would not make any difference. [608G H] 3. The prosecution has not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence in the case. It is not possible to adopt that course in assessing the quality of testimony of this solitary eye witness. [700H] 4. The mere fact that he stated in his first information Report that he was only mentioned the name or name of the assailant, does not make it a ground for conviction. [1008A B] 5. The Sessions Judge has not examined the injured witnesses who arrived at the place of occurrence and did not see the assailants whom they were present. It also stands to reason that those persons who gathered would not ask PW 4 to identify the assailants. There is no evidence in this case to show that the assailants, who had arrived at a little later than PW 4, did not know the assailants when he came to the place a little earlier than PW4. The other eye witnesses were not examined by the prosecution. [1108C D] 6. The trial court has not taken into consideration the intrinsic value of the testimony in court on a very material point. It has also come to the conclusion that the evidence given by the sole witness has not been corroborated by the contents of the FIR. [13E F] 7. The view taken by the High court is not even right that PW 4 stands wholly corroborated by his contents of FIR.

The respondent, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax in the hands of the respondents under section 34(1)(b) read with section 24B of the Income tax Act. The Income tax Officer found that the amounts received by the heirs and legal representatives were liable to pay out of the estate of the deceased, but the Tribunal held that the amount which was received subsequent to the previous year in which Amarchand died was liable to be taxed under section 24 B(1) (b). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the income which was actually received by him before his death and therefore the income received by them must be deemed by fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received in the previous years. HELD : The words "any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" mean that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income is received by his heirs and Legal representatives after his death, they are liable for payment of the tax just as the deceased would have be assessed to tax in respect of the amounts which were received by her husband. [707 D] The words 'any tax" in sub sections (1), (2) and (3) cannot be extended beyond the object for which it was enacted. In the present case, the fiction is limited to cases provided in the three clauses of section 24A and not to the liability for income received under the previous Act.

The Andhra Pradesh State and Subordinate Services (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959 were framed under the Act by the Central Government in exercise of powers conferred by section 3 of the Public Employment (R Equirement) Act, 1957. The petitioners who were members of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly filed petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the said rules and the validity thereof. The High Court dismissed their petition holding that the impugned rules were ultra vires the Constitution as they contravened article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners: (1) that the provisions of the Act are ultra vires, (2) that section 3 Of the Public employment (R handicirement), as to residence within the State or Union territory, and (3) that article 16(3) of the Constitu tion is violative of article 14. HELD : (i) The impugned rules are ultra rites and void. The provisions of section 3 are intra vires and must be struck down as invalid. [123 D] (ii) The power to make a law prescribing any requirement as to place residence within that State or any particular part of the State is not an absolute right but only an absolute one. It is not open to Parliament to enact a law which prescribes a condition precedent for making a declaration and leaving the details to be filled in by the rule making power of the Central or State Governments. [124 E] (iii) The provisions relating to residence in a particular part are ultra vivos, and they are ultravires. They are not ultra vires. [125 F G] (iv) The provision is valid because it does not provide for residence within a State or a Union territory. It cannot be said that the power is given to Parliament by law to make any law prescribing conditions as to residential qualification in a part of a State. [126 A B] (v) The word "any requirement" in article 14 means that the State must have a reasonable relation to the object sought to be achieved by the Constitution and not to the objects sought to achieve. It does not mean that the Legislature was aware of residence in parts of the States or Union territories.

The appellant was a postman attached to the appellant 's father. He was tried for offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code, and section 52 of the Act read with section 55 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The trial court convicted him but acquitted him on appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant, the appellant could not be said to have secreted the letter just because it was found in the almirah which was said to be in his exclusive possession. Held, that the mere fact that an officer of the post office had in the course of his duties access to postal articles kept or lying in the post offices, did not make any difference and could not justify the conclusion that he had secreted them from the post Office. The appellant was therefore entitled to be acquitted under section 52 without the Court having taken into consideration the evidence for satisfying itself as to the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions reached by the trial court. Held further, that in a case where the appellant had been able to prove his guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the mere circumstance that he was in possession of letters, that is what he could have done was not sufficient to show that he did not know the contents of the letter. The fact that the almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to the father and since he had the key with him it must be deemed to be the person who was in exclusive possession thereof.

The appellant, a Sarpanch of the Panchayat, was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 409 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ . The appeal against the conviction was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Sarpanch had not been properly authorised to administer oaths. It was also urged that the proceedings in the case were not proper and that the matter should be remanded to the Nyaya Panchayat for trial. HELD : The High Court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit was filed before the Nyaya Panchayats. [117 E] The High court was right in holding that the appellant had disobeyed an order of stay passed by it staying proceedings before the Tribunal. It is true that in certain cases, proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of court. [118 E] In the present case, the appellant did not have any opportunity to explain the allegations made in the application before him. It could not be said on the evidence that the High Courts had passed an order staying proceedings. The High Courts were therefore wrong in holding the enquiry and dealing with the evidence taken by them. [119 E] (ii) In the instant case, it was not proved that the Panchas had been properly sworn to or a certified copy of the order he urged that no contempt of Court has been established because a court is entitled not to act on an application which is not accompanied by an affidavit properly sworn. It may be true that the Magistrate had made an affidavit in his deposition that he had to authority to tell him that his affidavit was not proper.

The appellant was charged with the offence of murder under section 302 I.P.C., and was sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, Etawah. The High Court acquitted him but convicted him under section 307 I. P.C. and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the entire report of the police officer about the murder of Sheo Sahai was inadmissible in evidence as its contents did not amount to a confession of the offence by the appellant made to a Police Officer and that the evidence relied upon by the High Court was insufficient to establish conclusively that the appellant had committed the murder. HELD : (i)(a) The entire report was admissible under section 27 of the Evidence Act, and it is not necessary for the prosecution to prove that the accused had committed murder of the deceased or not. [209 B] (b) The evidence of the approver in his statement before the police Officer did not support the appellant 's statement. It was not possible to accept the statement made by the approver at the Police Station on the night of the murder and to examine him as a witness for the purpose of proving that he had committed it so soon after the murder, and that he could have made a statement that he knew that he was committing the murder in pursuance of the conspiracy. [210 C] (c) The extra judicial confession is admissible under s.27 of the Indian Evidence Act. It is not possible for the court to accept such evidence as it thinks fit. In the present case, the extra judicial confessions were made by a person who had enmity with him and was thereafter having a bath in his field. [211 E] (d) The statement of the accused that he did not commit the murder was inadmissible under section 25 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The evidence relied on by the trial court was insufficient in evidence to establish that the confession made by him was voluntary and was corroborated by Paley Singh, P.W. 13 who stated that the deceased had been taken to the Police station.

The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the electoral roll on the ground that they were not included in the electoral rolls and that they had been wrongly included in their electoral roll. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Rules, and that the notice was invalid as there was no proper explanation for the delay in filing the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the entire electoral roll had become void on account Of the defect of the notice; (ii) the period of 20 days had been mentioned in the notices issued under rule 4(2); and (iii) the declaration of results of election was invalid. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Collector has not given any explanation for delay in preferring claims or objections to file them within 30 days from the date of publication of the said notice. [419E] 2. The word "any person" in Rule 4 (1) is wide enough to include a person who is interested in preferring claim or objections against an election petition. It is not the case of the petitioners that they did not know immediately after the publication of such notice that in the said notices a period of 30 days had be given to them within the prescribed period. [519G H] 3. The expression "any other person" has been defined in section 2(g) of Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Act, 1951 and it is not necessary for any person to file his claim or objection to file it within 30 day from the time specified in the proviso to Rule 4. [511B C] 4. The notice issued by the Collector under Rule 3(1), as required by Rule 4 of the Madhya Pradesh Rules, must be read as a whole and not merely one part of the record of the proceedings. It cannot be said that the petitioners were entitled to the issue of the writ prayed for as of right and the delay was not condoned. [55H] 5. The petition is therefore rightly dismissed by the High court as there is no satisfactory explanation for not filing the petition till December 28, 1978 even though they knew that there was an error in the proceedings issued under r. 4(3) of Rules.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1956. The Directors of the company were appointed as directors of the Company and their names were entered in the register of the Companies. The appellant company filed a complaint against the appellant company for failure to comply with the requirements of section 220(1) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913 or section 220 of the . The appellant contended that the company was not liable under the provisions of section 134(4) of that Act as no balance sheet was laid before a general body, there could be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirement of section 221(1). The High Court held that the appellant had failed to comply within the requirements Of section 220 and since no balance sheets were prepared by the company in accordance with the provisions contained in section 220 (1) the company and its directors could not rely upon their failure to call the general meeting as a defence to the prosecution. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The appellant was guilty of contravention of section 135(1)(3). [415 B] The charge under sections 134(2) and 220(3) of Indian Companies is for default in filing copies of the balance sheet or profit and loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act. Under section 131(1), if no balance Sheet is adopted at the general meetings, there can be no doubt that no copy of the entire balance sheet so laid before the general body may have been forwarded under sub section (2) of section 132 or sub section(3). But section 134 lays down that after balance sheet and profit and Loss account are filed, a statement of that fact and of the reasons therefore has to be annexed to the balance sheets and profit. [416 C D] In the present case, the appellant was not guilty of any contravention of the provisions under section 135 (1). [414 E F] The appellant had not complied with the required requirements of Section 220(2), but only made a statement in respect of the general election to the Board of Directors. It is true that the requirement to send a copy of such documents is not mandatory and the failure to do so is an obligation to file the list under section 131 (1)( 3). [416 G H] In view of the fact that section 26 makes the offence a continuing one also shows that the obligation to send the copy of balance sheet is dependent completely on its being laid before it at the General meeting. The intention is made further clear by the provision under sub s.(2) which provides that after the balance Sheet and profit, and loss accounts are submitted, the balance Sheets and profit or loss account are dependent entirely on its having been laid before such meeting. [416 A B] In re : Hutchinson (1893) L.R. 59 I.A. 65; Hutcheson (1924) L R. 60 I. A. 76; Hurmull vs Hurman, ; , referred to.

The appellants were convicted by the Special Court under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1947. The appellants contended that the provisions of the Act were discriminatory and violative of article 14 Of the Constitution inasmuch as they had been deprived of their fundamental rights guaranteed to them by articles 19(1)(f), 19(2) and 31(3) of India Act, 1935, and that the classification was based on a reasonable classification. Held, (per Sinha, C. J., Das Gupta and Shah, JJ.) that the object of the impugned Act was to provide for speedier trial of certain offences or classes of cases and not to make them more effective than those by ordinary courts. The provisions of section 5 (1) were intended to be in conformity with the principles laid down in the preamble to the Act as a whole, and the object being to provide a speedy trial of all offences or class of cases or classes thereof, it was necessary to ascertain whether it is actually based on such a classification. The object of section 4(1), read with section 5 of the Bengal Special courts Act, 1946, was to make a distinction between those cases and those in which they were intended for the purpose of making them more favourable than those in whose case the procedure prescribed by the Code had been followed. The scheme of the provisions contained in the Act showed that it was not possible to ascertain what is actually done under the provisions Of the Act, but only whether the procedure laid down therein was discriminatory or violative of articles 14 and 19(5) of Constitution. The classification made by the impugned section was based upon a reasonable differentia which had a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by it and that differentia must have a rational nexus with the object intended to achieve. The Act did not contravene article 14 of the Constitution as it purported to impose a reasonable restriction on the fundamental rights under articles 19 (1)(g) and 19 (5). The classification was therefore, valid in so far as it authorised the State Government to direct "cases" to be tried by a Special Court according to the procedure provided by it for the speediers trial. The fact that the Act did no more than provide for a speedior trial of those offences or cases or class or classes or cases was not relevant to the question whether the classification made in the impugned statute was discriminatory and therefore violative of Article 14 Of Constitution.

The appellant, a doctor in the Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules, 1966, was appointed as an Assistant Professor of Radiology in the Medical College. The appellant was appointed to the post of Associate Professor of radiology in a teaching hospital. He was also appointed to that post on the recommendation of a Departmental Promotion Committee. The respondent, who was working as an Associate Professor in the Hospital, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the appointment of the appellant as a Professor of Pathologist in the M.D. Medical College and claimed that he had been appointed to a post of Assistant Professor in Radiology (ex officio) in the Health Department of Health and Family Planning Department of the Health Ministry of Health, and that the appellant could not be considered for appointment to the said post as an Professor of the Radiologist. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the post was a teaching post and that it was a research post which was a subject matter of the writ petition. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the qualifications prescribed for the post were different and the appellant who had been substantively appointed to post of Professor of Hospital was not entitled to be considered as an officer of the University of Delhi in view of the fact that he did not possess at least five years ' teaching experience as Reader/Assistant Professor in a research college. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The post of a Radiologist cum Associate Professor is a teaching institution attached to the Maulana Azad Medical College which is a post belonging to Specialists Grade II, cannot be appointed by direct recruitment as Professor of an Institute of Radiologist or a Professor in any other University like a research institution attached thereto. [802C] 2. The qualifications prescribed by the First Schedule are different and they are not identical. The nature of the duties of the post is different and there is no difference between the two posts of Radiologists and the post in which the post has fallen vacant in 1973. [8803D] 3. The status of the Appellant as a Radiological post is a research job, and it cannot be said that the Appellant has not acquired the status of an Associate Professors of Radiological College with effect from October 9, 1964. [902E] 4. The question whether the appellant had acquired the degree of the doctor in a medical college which was affiliated to the Munici pal University or was a Research Institute under the provisions of the Central health Service (Second Schedule) Act, 1966 is not relevant because the qualifications for such promotion or appointment are different. [8903G] 5. The qualification prescribed by Section 2(b) of the Act is that a person who has been substantively employed to the service of an institution in a college which is affiliated to a specialists Grade I will be eligible to be appointed as Professor or Associate Professor, and if not, whether the person is eligible for appointment as Professor. [9003G H] 6. The degree of experience given by the appellant is not equivalent to that of Honorary Professor or Assistant Professor. It is also not necessary that the degree should have been possessed by an officer in a hospital which is not a research College attached to it. [91F] 7. The fact that the respondent had acquired a status of a doctor with effectfrom October 9 1964 cannot be taken into consideration. [92G] 8. The requirement of experience for such appointment or appointment is different from the post under the First schedule. The letter dated February 23, 1974 issued by the Central Government to the appellant clearly shows that the three posts of Assistant Professors were different. The two posts are distinct and separate. The respondents have been appointed as Assistant Professor and Assistant Professor respectively in the Specialists ' Grade I. [93A] 8(2) The qualifications for appointment are distinct from those under the first schedule.

The appellant company was a registered company under the , and its workmen were paid minimum wages in respect of certain categories of workmen. The workmen claimed that they should be paid minimum wage at the rate of three months basic wages, dearness allowance, dearness allowances, dearness Allowance, dearness pay, dearness and other allowances, and dearness allowance. The Tribunal held that there was no similar industry in the region where minimum wages were higher than the minimum wages fixed by the company, but failed to fix the minimum wage in accordance with the minimum rates of wages. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the minimum pay in the Company 's case was not uniform and it was not necessary that the basic wage should be fixed at Rs. 95. The appellant contended that the workmen were providing any such amenities which are different from those amenities which were being provided by those concerns in the State, and that the tribunal had erred on this ground. HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding the minimum of wages as a result of the award of the Industrial Tribunal. [678C] (ii) The workmen and the Company have agreed to exclude them from the purview of the circumstances of the case, and the Tribunal was justified in basing its decision on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of 1959. [689D] (iii) The appellant 's contention that the appellant should be given full effect to the principle laid down by this Court in the Associated Cement Companies Ltd. vs Their Workmen, ; , is not correct. The fact that the workers are provided any such facilities which are distinct from those facilities which were available to them in the area which are being used for the purpose of fixing the minimum rate of wages does not make it a condition precedent for fixing the maximum wage. [699D E] (iv) The principle laid by this court is that to give full effect, the Tribunal should have proceeded to fix minimum wage and dearness allowances. In such cases, the calculation is still on the basis of basic wage. The principle which is being applied is the simple one of calculating the bonus payable at the rates of three month ' basic wages. [709E] (v) The award of this Court is not based on any principle of law requiring interference by this Tribunal in its award. [71H; 72A] (vi) The principles which are to be applied are well settled and they have to be considered in the light of the principles laid down in the later Agreement of 1958.

The appellant was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 19 19 19 20. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961 on the ground that it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act and that the impugned notice was invalid as it didnot comply with section 151 (2). The appellant challenged the validity of the said notice by means of a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the notice was valid because it did neither contain any reason for coming to the conclusion that this was a fit case for the issue of a notice. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order sheet recording reasons of the Income tax officer as required by section 148(2), is not sufficient for the appellant to have given an opportunity to make a return under section 139 for any assessment year. [448 B] (ii) The High court was right in holding that it was a proper case to issue notice under s 148. 148. [449 C D] (iii) The notice dated June 3, 1966 did not set out any reason why the impugned notices should be quashed. The order sheets recording reasons for doing so were not produced. [453 B] In the present case the affidavit filed by the Income Tax Officer to be vague and indefinite, was not sufficient to enable him to make an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [454 C D]. (iv) The appellant did not himself record that he was satisfied that this is a fit cases for the issuance of a show cause notice under Section 148. He did not itself record that the appellant was satisfied with this requirement.

The appellant was a partner in a partnership firm which carried on business in the manufacture of iron and steel products. The Income tax Officer, after assessing the appellant as income from the profits and gains of the previous year, assessed him to income tax for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the business must have been charged to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918 and that the assessee was not liable to pay tax on the income, profits and losses of the firm. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The assessment for the year 1948 49 was made in 1948 and the assessment for 1949 50 was made on April 1, 1939, and the appellant was assessed under the Act of 1918. The assessment was not made on March 28, 1939 but on April 13, 1939. The income tax authorities were therefore entitled to the benefit of section 25(3) of the Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939 which came into force on April 14, 1939 when the Indian Finance Act, 1948 came into effect. (ii)The appellant had been assessed under that Act for the assessment year 1948 50 and 1949 51 as a result of which the income tax was charged under the provisions of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. The appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 25 (3). The Income Tax Officer was therefore entitled under section 26(2) to the benefits of section 26 (4) on the ground that the income of the appellant had escaped assessment and the assessee could not be assessed for the period between April 13 , 1938 and March 28. (iii)The question whether the income in question was liable to tax for this year was a matter which fell within the scope of section 2(3).

The appellant, a co sharer of the joint family property, was allotted to his wife and son in equal shares. The appellant 's father died in 1945 leaving behind his widow and son. The respondent filed a suit for partition claiming that there was no prior partition and that the appellant had no right to a share in the coparcenary property. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal of the appellant holding that the suit properties belonged to the joint Hindu Mitakshara coparcener and that there were four sharers in the joint property, that there had been no prior division and that it was not possible for the respondent to prove that the partition was effected between him and his two sons. The High Court also held that the plaintiff 's share must be ascertained by adding the share to which she is entitled at a notional partition during her husband 's life time and the share which she would get in her husband"s property under section 10 read with Rules 1 and 2 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (i) the suit property belonged to joint family and that as the appellant was entitled to a 723 share in his coparcenary property, the interest of the deceased in the Mitakshara property would devolve by survivorship upon the surviving members of the coparcenary and not in accordance with the provisions of the Act; (ii) the plaintiff was entitled only to a 1/4th share in her joint family properties under section 8 read with Rule 1 and2 of that rule. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The suit property belongs to the Joint Hindu Mitakshara coparcenary and therefore, the appellant 'S 's interest must be determined according to the terms of the testamentary instrument, if any, made by the deceased and since there is none in the instant case, by the application of the rules of intestate succession contained in sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Indian Succession Act. [724G] (i). The rule that a Hindu Mitakshara Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death. In a partition between a member of a joint family, a partition is effected between himself and his sons, there would be four sharer in the undivided family property at the time of his death, in addition to the share that he or she received or must be deemed not to have been entitled to claim partition or not. [764B C] (ii).

The appellant Corporation was a Corporation established under the Employees ' State Insurance Act, 1948. The Corporation framed regulations for the establishment of an Industrial Tribunal for the purpose of determining the age of retirement of employees in Class I and Class II. The appellant Corporation filed writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of regulation 19(2) of the Regulations on the ground that the Corporation had no power to make any regulation under section 49(2). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the regulations were not applicable to the employees who became employees of Class I or Class II and therefore they could not be reduced to 58 years of age. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the Regulations were in terms applicable to employees who had become employees of class I or class II and since the regulations did not apply to them, they could only be treated as having been made applicable to them. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The regulations are statutory rules and the regulations framed by the Corporation under section 11 of the Act. They are statutory regulations and the Regulations are statutory ones. [223D] 2. The Regulations do not provide for any regulation or regulation of the employees of the Corporation on the one hand under the settlement and the amendment made in the Regulations by the new sub regulation (2) thereof empowered the appointing authority to extend at its discretion the service of any employee of the Corpora tion on the other hand under section II of the , but only referred to the employee and employees of a corporation. [225E] 3. The Regulation is not applicable in respect of persons who were appointed directly to any post belonging to Class I nor class II or class III categories. It is only in 1965 that the employees are given the benefit of the age prescribed for them. In other words, the regulations do not apply. [226F G] 4. The regulation is a statutory rule and the regulation cannot be said to have been made by the Regulations. The rules do not contain any provision for any alteration or amendment of the regulations in the regulations. It does not provide that the age should be fixed at 58 years. [227G H] 5.

The appellants were charged with contempt of court. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that they had not been given an opportunity to show cause against the order of dismissal. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that there was no intention whatsoever on their part to scandalise the Hon 'ble Judge or the Court in any manner to weaken people 's faith in the administration of justice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contempt is a matter of discretion and not of a Judge. It is an article of faith with the deponent that the Judges are expected to be a finding of committal of contempt. [243C] 2. In order to prevent unwanted disclosure of its contents, the communication in question was brought personally by two members of the Bar Association, Bhiwani to Chandigarh in a closed cover addressed to the Chief Justice for being handed over to him for his personal attention. The letter did not mention which particular portion of the letter constituted contempt of Court. [244D] 3. In view of this fact that the High Court proceeded on the basis that the allegations in the letter were admitted and that the contents of the letters constituted contempt, the Chief justice of India was not in keeping with the well accepted role of a judge. The appellant had no concern to scandalising the Hon`ble Judge nor did he have any occasion for acceptance of apology. [245E] 4. In the absence of such a finding no question arises for acceptance.

The petitioner, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The petitioner challenged the validity of section 5(1) of the Act on the ground that it contravened article 14 of the Constitution and as such the impugned Act violated articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of Constitution. Held, (per Sinha C. J., Sarkar and Das Gupta JJ.) that the provisions of section 34 of the Indian Incometax Act were not discriminatory in nature and were void under article 14 Of the Constitution. The provisions of the impugned section are not discriminatory and do not offend against articles 14 or 19(2) of India. The impugned Act was therefore ultra vires as it contravened articles 14, 19(5), 31(1), 31 (3) and 31(4). The impugned order was therefore void under articles 14 of Constitution and must be struck down. Per Sarkar C.J., Das Gupta and Das JJ. (dissenting) The provisions in section 5 (1) and (2) are not violative of article 14 because they are discriminatory and are, therefore, invalid. The Act is a piece of discriminatory legislation which is not discriminatory. The object of the two Acts was to provide for the same class of persons as were mentioned in section 34 Of the Indian income tax Act and under the provisions Of section 5 of the said Act it is not limited to any period and this is not violative by article 14. The validity of the provisions relating to taxation on income, profits or evaded income is limited to a maximum period of eight years, while under the provision of section 4(1). The provisions contained in section 6(5) are discriminatory as they are inconsistent with the provisions contained therein and are therefore void. Per Das Gupta J. (Concurring) The impugned legislation was not discriminatory but was within the scope of article 19(6) of that Constitution. It is well settled that the impugned law must be held to be invalid under article 19 (5) of our Constitution. There is no doubt that there is in this matter a discrimination between persons proceeded against under section 34 and those who were not being investigated under that sub section, but they are also subjected to discriminatory treatment even from those whose cases are referred to under section 5. The classification made by the impugned legislation is based on intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons grouped together in one group or groups of different classes and is thus invalid. It cannot be said that there was discrimination between members of a class and members of the same group.

The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, New Delhi was established in the year 1956. The Federation of India was a " commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act. The Association was registered under the . The Federation was registered as an "commercial establishment". The Federation filed a writ petition challenging the order of the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the activities of the Federation were not "a business or trade" within its meaning and that the activity of the Association was not "business" within section 2 (5) Of the Act, which in consequence had no application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the services of the respondent were not ' commercial establishment ' within the definition of "commercial Establishment". Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The activities of a Federation are not "industrial" and therefore, they cannot be said to be "business or trade". [352 B] The activity of this Court in the context of "industry" is primarily for the purpose of carrying on of business. It is not necessary that the business should be carried on by it amounts to a commercial establishment. [353 C] The activities are connected with trade and business, generally. The activities which are connected or incidental or ancillary to trade or business in general within the latter part of the definition. [352 E] In the instant case, the activity was not 'a commercial establishment but an association of individuals, industrialists and businessmen. It was a commercial activity of profession within the purview of section2(5). The activities were connected with the trade and commerce. [351 G] The expression "business", in section 2 of the is wide enough to include "business". The word 'business ' has been defined in the Act as meaning "a commercial activity" in section 3(1) of that Act. It would be a commercial one. [354 E] The definition of 'industry ' in section2 (j) of this Act does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. [355 G] In view of the fact that the respondent was a 'trade, business ' within its ambit and as such it was not an 'establishment ' within section 3 (1). [354 F] The word "business " in section 1(5), means "a trade or trade or commerce". It is only when there is a profit that the said activity is carried on in a premises that amounts to business, then the activity carried on must be carried out by it.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of two sons, one of whom was the original founder and owner. The income from the property was appropriated by him as his remuneration for management of the trust properties. The Income tax Officer held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer but on further revision, the High Court held that from the language of the letter dated July 7, 1837, it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. The High Court also held that the income from property was not agricultural income for "valuing" the assessee 's estate and did no longer fall within section 4(3)(viii) of the Act. In appeal by certificate, HELD: (i) The source of the pension is a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of income was not land or rent collections from land, it is difficult to hold that the receipt of the appellant was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4 (3)(vii). [702 D] (ii) The income of a trust appropriated by the appellant as his agent was not in the right to receive rent or revenue of agricultural lands but was in the nature of a grant made by him. [703 G H] (iii) The allowance is revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income. It follows from the decisions of this Court that if it is held in this case that the source of pension or pension is the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and, therefore, it cannot be said that the payment was in fact a payment in instalments of the value of the disputed title of the asses see. [700 C] (iv) The appellant 's claim for exemption from taxation under section 4 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 is not agricultural land as defined in the Act and therefore it is not agriculture income.

The petitioners in C.A. No. 441 of 1981 were appointed as Supervisors 'A ' in various ordnance factories between 1962 to 1966. The petitioners in the writ petitions filed before the Madhya Pradesh High Court claimed that they had been appointed as Supervisor 'A" by promotion from the date of their initial appointment and that they should be treated as Chargeman II on completion of 2 years ' service on the basis of seniority cum seniority. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioners were not entitled to be considered for promotion merely on completion Of 2 years of continuous service on 1st January, 1966. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since Rule 8 of the Rules contemplated th at appointments by promotion were to be made on the principle of seniority and not on the completion of two years ' continuous service, the High Court should have taken into consideration the length of service as a matter of fact. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The State Government has no power to make any order for promo tion merely because it is made by promotion or by way of promotion. [408C] 2.1 Rule 8(a) of the Madhya Prade ry Rules contemplated that there should be no por tive appointment in the same manner as provided therein. The rule was not intended to confer any right on the State Government to make an order for promotion only on completion oth er of two yea rs of service, and his promotion thereafter could be effected only in accordance with the normal rules. [441G] 2:2 In the instant case, the appellants of this appeal have in pur poses sion that they were appointed on the same day as Supervisor/A ' by its order dated 16th April, 1983. The appellants of these appeals are not entitled t he benefit of Rule 8. [442C D] 3.1 The State has no right to make such an order. It is only when a person will not be entitled to any p ay and allowance during the period for which he did not know about it, that he will not have been promoted as Chargemen in or about the year 19 66 he chose to wait for about 17 years to file these petitions which were filed after the decision of this Court dated 2nd February, 1981 in Civil Appeal No. 442 of 1981 in CAs Nos. 441/81 and 441/1981. [443E F] 3:2 The State is directed that the appellants shall be given the benefit of promotion only from the dates they did not possess any other qualification.

Singh ' case and that it had not been shown that the decision given by the Tribunal was erroneous. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The view taken in Sher Sing Singh ' Case is correct and must be upheld. [1006A B] Sher Singh vs Union of India & Ors., ; , referred to. 2.2 The High court was wrong in not considering the merits and the reasons given by it for rejecting the claims.
