The respondent was a dealer in the business of selling and selling goods. The Sales Tax Officer, who assessed the appellant to sales tax under section 19(1) of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, levied sales tax on the turnover of the respondent. The respondent filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner which was dismissed by the Appellate Tribunal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the power of the State Government under section 9(1). HELD : (i) The word 'assessment ' used in section 19 (2)(c) does not include the power to recover tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule 22A is beyond the rule making power of State Government either under section19(1), or section 19. [665 B] (ii) The expression 'assessment" used in Section 19(2)(C) doesnot include the powers of recovery of tax assessed to sales Tax only in respect of his turnover and under the scheme of the charging provision of the Act the purchaser of the business has nothing to do with the sales effected by the seller of the goods. [664 E] (iii) The words 'assessment " in section 9 (1) and (2) are wide enough to include the right of recovery and payment of tax from some other person other except a "dealer" under the Act. [663 F G] (iv) Rule 21A is ultra vires the rule made by the State Govern ment under section 10(1)(c). The word "assessment" in section 18(2) (c) has not been used in the sense of 'assessment". [665 H] (v) The High Court was right in holding that Rule 23 A is beyond its rule making powers of the state Government either tinder section 19 or section 20(2).

The appellant was a contractor. He entered into an agreement with the State of Gujarat for the supply of water from the appellant 's factory to the appellant. The contract provided that the appellant would be liable to pay arrears of salary and allowances during the period of his employment. The appellant claimed that he continued to be in Government service till the date of the suit only and there was no duty to supply a copy of the report of the enquiry held against him. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court on appeal confirmed the decree. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the High court erred in holding that there had been a breach of article 311(2) of the Constitution and as such the liability arising out of a contract could not be enforced against the State. HELD : (i) The High Court erred in ordering payment of arrears of pay to the respondent. [922 B] (ii) The appellant was not concerned with the second contention but it was a dispute between the State and the State which was one of the parties. It is true that the State Government of Bombay had made any contract in the exercise of its executive power for any purposes of the State, that contract would be deemed to have been made in the discharge of the executive power, (iii) The State of Bombay vs The Province of Bombay, ; , relied on. (iv) The liability arising from a contract within section 60(2)(a) of Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, is not a liability in respect of an actionable wrong other than a breach Of contract.

The appellants were the owners of a colliery. The respondents claimed that they had encroached upon their land and that they were entitled to the reliefs prayed for by them. The trial court held that the respondent was not barred by limitation, but decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court reversed the findings of the courts below and dismissed the suit holding that the respondents had encroached on the land in question. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts were wrong in holding that they could not claim the reliefs claimed for. Held, that the decision of the High court was correct. The High Court was right in holding (i) that the suit was barred by limitations and that the courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit; (ii) that under the rules of evidence the respondents were bound to keep a barrier of 25 feet to the south of the defendant 's working and, therefore, the coal that is still left in the encroached area was not by any means available to the plaintiffs. The rule of evidence is based on the assumption that the initial burden was on the respondents to prove that they have knowledge of the said encroachment only within three years of the suit, and that is all. Held further, that under section 3(b) of the Indian Coal Mines Regulation, 1946, the respondents could claim the relief claimed for the reliefs sought for by the appellants. The fact that the coal still left the encroached land was not a matter of statutory obligation on the part of the plain. It was clear from the language of the rule that the parties must prove that he obtained the knowledge of it and being thus wholly unworkable is entirely lost to them for ever.

The appellant was a workman in Kozihkode. He was suspended from service by an order dated June 25, 1958. The appellant challenged the suspension on the ground that it was mala fide exercise of the power conferred under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders and having taken action under r, 18(b) of that Standing Orders, he was not competent to dismiss him. He also contended that the enquiry was vitiated by victimisation or unfair labour practice. The Tribunal held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r 18(c). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order terminating the services of the respondent was mala fides and was not bona fide exercise Of the power under that rule. HELD : (i) The Tribunal had the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(1) of Standing Orders. It is well settled that in view of the decision of this Court in the case of this kind the requirement of bona fide action under section 10(a), by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action taken under such a rule was a colourable exercise of power and was, therefore, not bona fides. [824 D E] (ii) The employer could defend the action under the Standing orders without holding any departmental inquiry and the order was passed mala fide. The tribunal had the power to inquire whether the action proposed was mala or unfair Labour practice. It was not open to the Tribunal to inquire as to whether the enquiry should be held. [924 F] (iii) The appellant failed to satisfy the Tribunal when it came before it for adjudication that the exercise of powers under r., 18(d) was a bona fide exercised and was therefore mala fide or was a result of victimisation or illegal labour practice it would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. [936 G] (iv) The tribunal could not inquire into any cause which led to the termination of services under r; 18(e). It is open to an employer to take action for misconduct and then initiate disciplinary proceedings which were intended to be held and decided to discharge the employee under r: 18(i) if it is satisfied that the action was made mala fide, or unfair, labour practice, it would not have jurisdiction. [951 G H] (v) The order terminating services of an employee and has not been accepted by industrial tribunals over a long course of years now and the view taken by industrial Tribunals in this case is correct.

The appellant, a cinematograph theatre, was granted a licence to the respondent for running a cinema. The licence was renewed from time to time by the Bombay Municipal Corporation on November 27, 1954. On November 27. 1955, the respondent filed an application under section 47 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, for permission to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. The trial court held that the agreement dated November 27 was not a lease but a lease and that the consent decree was not binding on the respondent. On appeal by special leave, the High Court set aside the order of the Trial Court and directed the trial court to proceed with the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that an enquiry into the nature of the legal relationship arising out of the agreement between the parties was a matter to be decided by the Court and on which the opinion of witnesses was irrelevant. HELD: (i) The question whether in fact the subordinate court has decided the question and there after the High Courts have decided it is not open to the appellant in revision at this stage to express any opinion about the rights and contentions of the parties with reference to the agreement of December 1, 1960. [446 B] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the suit was barred by the principle of res judicata. [441 C D] (iii) The finding of the trial Court that the appellant had not decided that the transaction between the respondent of the year 1954 was in the nature or a lease, was not correct. [442 E] (iv) The agreement dated December 1. 1960 created a lease. It was for the Trial court to decide whether the agreement was a lease or of other character. If it was not so, then the question whether the parties were entitled to raise an issue as to the validity of the contract would be decided at the trial and the previous judgment being a judgment by consent, the Court has no jurisdiction on principles of resjudicata to go into that question.

The respondent was appointed as a pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was working as a Pilot Officer. He was confirmed in service on 30th August, 1985 by an order dated 1st June, 1983. If the respondent had not been extended by 30th October, 1985 he should have preferred an appeal before this Court and that the order passed in his case was not on the other hand he proceeded to file a Review Petition claiming to be re spondent for being reinstated in serv ice. [245E F] 1 :4. The interim order that had been passed on 10.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of death. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the prosecution case was that the deceased was the wife of the deceased; (ii) the evidence of P.W. 1 to 3 was not corroborated by any independent evidence; (iii) the discrepancies noticed by the Sessions Judge were of a minor character and that the High Court should not interfere with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The prosecution case against the appellant must be reasonable and not in the least probable. [368E] In the instant case, the evidence was so strong against the accused. It was clear that the witnesses were interested witnesses. They were closely related to the deceased and their relations with the deceased. There was no reason to doubt the testimony of P W. 1. 2 to 3 or that the evidence in the case was one based on circumstantial evidence. [369E] The High Courts should not disturb the order unless it is shown that the accused person has any motive for killing his wife and that he has been unduly magnified by the learned Sessions Judge. [370G] Khem Karan & Ors. vs State of U.P., ; , referred to. In the present case, there was no evidence to show that the appellant had any motive to kill his wife. The prosecution story was not supported by any reliable evidence. It is true that the prosecution witnesses were closely associated with the accused and their evidence was corroborated by some independent evidence. But the High Courts have failed to appreciate that the discrepancies on the basis of which the Trial Court rejected the evidence, of P,W. 3 and the evidence given by the prosecution were of no consequence. [367A B] Khem Raj & Ors vs State, ; , followed. Khem Karan and Anr. vs The State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr., ; ; Khem Karan vs State Of U. P.

The appellant, a Judge of the High Court, was convicted and sentenced to death under section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court dismissed his appeal by special leave against the conviction and sentence. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the case of a Judge or Chief Justice of the Supreme Court; (ii) the provision in clause (e) had to be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, inasmuch as the High Courts had no jurisdiction to try the case; and (iii) the power to punish a Judge under section 6(1) (c) was not available to the appellant because of the provisions contained in clauses (4) and (5) of Article 124 read with article 124(4). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "any provision" in clause(e) has to be interpreted in a broad sense and should be given an extended meaning which will include not only the provisions relating to the procedure for removal of a judge but also the provisions regarding the procedure to be followed by him. [216C] 2.1 The word "shall" used in clauses 4 and 5 of Article 123(4) is wide enough to cover all cases where the trial and punishment are involved. It is not necessary that the words "may" should be read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which the disproportion and his inability to satisfactorily account can be inferred. The word 'shall ' in clause 4(4), even for investigation and proof of any misbehaviour alleged against a superior Judge, instead of the general law was clearly visualised when the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office. [217D E] 2:2 In the instant case, the provisions in clauses 3 and 5 are clear enough to show that the provisions were intended to be complied with by the competent authority to grant sanction for prosecution of a person holding such an office. The fact that the Parliament did not enact any other law even then for the investigation into allegations of corruption against a subordinate Judge or the Chief Justice, would not necessarily apply to the Judges of the Court. [218H; 218A] 3:3 The word `shall ' is used in clause 2(e), which has to he read as an integral part of it and not in any manner whatsoever. It cannot be said that the expression "shall", in clause 3(c) has been used in the context under which it was intended to include a Judge, or Chief justice of a High Court. The words 'may" in cl. (e), have to be read ejusdem generis with the word 'may ' and not merely the word `may '. [220D E; 221A] 4:1. The use of the expression 'shall" in clauses 2(a) and 2(b) of sub section (1) of Section 6 in the present case, is in pari materia with clause (c). [222F] 5:2. The provisions in clause 1(e)(i) have to he given some interpretation which would indicate that the word "may", has been understood when the said provision was enacted by Parliament under Article 124(5), even if it were read as part of a scheme under Section 6(I)(c). The words "shall be deemed to be the authority to give effect to the provisions for the procedure prescribed in clause 5(2) are not intended to cover the proceedings before the Court of the Chief justice. [222G H] 3.1.

The appellant was a member of the Saha caste. He was declared elected to the West Bengal Legislative Assembly from the Khargram Murshidabad, as a result of an election held in the West Pakistan. The respondent challenged the election on the ground that he belonged to a smaller caste and not a member thereof. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had been a member and was therefore not entitled to be declared elected. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that as the appellant belonged to the "Sad" community, he could not be declared a member under section 3(1)(a) of the West Benitta Act, 1949 and that the respondent had been declared a 'Sad '. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding the appellant to be a member. [390 B] (ii) The word "Safal" in the expression "including Sahas". "Sah" in section 3 of the Act means "a person who has been declared to be an individual". If the correct interpretation of item 40 is that it indicates men of the Sunri caste, a particular group within the Sunhar caste cannot be regarded as a distinct and independent class independent of the S.C.R. [391 C] (iii) The appellant was not a 's name ' in the Schedule to the Order. He did not belong to the S Hindu community within the meaning of section 3 (1)(b). [390 G H] (iv) The expression "Sabah" is used in the sense that it includes "a particular group". It means a person who is declared as an individual and has not been proved to belong to a larger caste. If the true interpretation of the item is that the word 'Safals ' in section 2(1) (b) must be construed as meaning that it would include those who are included within the definition of "Sapah".

The appellant was a partner of the respondent firm. The appellant entered into an agreement with the appellant for the supply of electric energy to the appellant and the latter agreed to pay Rs. 29,500 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs. 2,000 for the furniture and that the appellant was not entitled to any further sum or consideration as a condition of the relin quishment by the respondent. The trial court found that the agreement was not genuine and that it was not lawful for the tenant to pay the amount of the additional amount. On appeal the High Court held that the transaction was not valid because the appellant had agreed to accept the offer made by the appellant in favour of the appellant, and that he was in possession of a flat and that there was no agreement between him and the appellant. Held, that the contract was not a term of art and was used in the section for the purpose of carrying on the business of the tenant and as such it could not be said that the respondent was in fact a lawful occupation of the premises. The mere fact that the parties were parties to the agreement did not make any difference. The agreement was intended by the legislature to give effect to the intention of the parties. The intention of a party to an assignment is not necessary, in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary. The consent of the landlord to an assign is not required in the present case. The word "relinquishment" used in section 18(1) of the Act would have been more appropriate.

The appellants were working as Draughtsmen and Rs. 100/ in the category of Draughtsmen. The Tribunal held that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a rational basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. In appeal by special leave, the appellants contended that the new wage scales had been fixed in the revised pay scale with reference to the existing wages and dearness allowance, and that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the old wage scales could not be applied to the present case because the increase in the basic pay of individual workman was intended in the original wage structure. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The new wage structure is a statutory one and it cannot be said that the change in the existing scale of pay has been made to rest. [183B] 2. The old wage structure has been introduced by the Government with effect from 1st April, 1976. It is not possible for any flat or ad hoc increase of salary to all employees except those who were to get additional pay of Rs. 150/ and Rs 100/ as the existing pay scales. The existing wage scale had necessarily to be fixed in accordance with the existing scales. [184D] 3. The revised wage structure was intended to apply to each individual workman, there is nothing in the body of the award to form the foundation on which the actual figures in the restructured pay scales can be made to be taken into account. [185E F] 4. The change in paragraph 22 of the Award is not a matter of law but of fact. It cannot be the case of the union that the figure of Rs 150/ was intended by the Tribunal as is evident from the reference to "flat increase of Rs 100" in the initial pay scale of Rs, 150/ in case of other categories. [186F] 5. The award in the instant case did not contain any provision for giving any ad hoc enhancement of salary and dearness allowances to all the employees in the case. It was clearly so intended by it as is apparent from the award that all the workmen were to be given additional pay at the revised scales of pay, it would obviously result in serious anomalous situations. [187G H] 6. The increase in basic pay scale was not a condition precedent for making any change in its structure. It could not therefore be said to have been made by the tribunal as is manifest from the Award that all employees were to receive additional pay and dearness Allowance, and there was no mention of giving any additional financial advantage to the Union. [188H; 189A] 7. The fact that the workmen raised industrial disputes for revision of wage scales is certainly not a ground for interference with the award. [189B C] 8. The Industrial Tribunal thought that an all round flat increase of pay was just and reasonable, and therefore it fell into the error of amending the award in making the award dated December 20, 1978. [ 189E F; 190A] 9. The High Court was wrong on the ground that the award did not give any ad interim relief to the workmen.

The appellant was a registered firm carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling textiles. The appellant paid wages for the period from 1st April, 1948 to 31st March, 1948. The workmen claimed that they were entitled to wages at the rate of Rs. 10 per day and in addition to the wages payable by them under section 2(vi) of the Act. The Industrial Tribunal held that the wages prescribed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed under section2(vi). The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The provisions of section 2 (vi) and 2(vii) of Act, 1958, are applicable to the case because the rates of wages fixed by the Award do not fall under the definition. [421 B] (ii) The expression "wages" in section 2 of the Industrial Disputes Act is not a term of employment prescribed by an award but it includes wages which would be payable. [420 C D] (iii) The definition of Wages Act, 1948, does not take in the wages fixed under the award. The definition in section 3(vi), as it stood at the relevant time, provides that wages means all remuneration, capable of being expressed in terms of money, which would, if the terms of the contract of employment, express or implied, were fulfilled, be payable; and so, it has to be read as a whole. [416 D E] (iv) The words " wages" in the definition are not intended to include wages fixed for wages fixed in section 23(1). [422 G H] (v) The word 'wages ' is used in the context of industrial adjudication and not in any sense, it means wages which are payable. It is not defined as a term in the Act but in the sense of wages.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was prosecuted under section 465 and section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed an offence punishable under section 467 read with section 409 I.P.C., and was convicted by the trial court. The High Court held that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been obtained under section 196(1), Cr. P.C. and that there having been an acquittal of the appellant by the Trial Court, the prosecution could be prosecuted under s. 465 and the conviction was set aside. The appellant contended that sanction was necessary for prosecuting him under section 198(1). Held, that sanction is necessary only when it is shown that the offence had been committed while the accused was actually engaged in the performance of his official duties; but if sanction under that section is necessary, as contended for by the respondent, the sanction under s 197(2) of Code of criminal Procedure would be necessary. The sanction under sec. 197( 1) of Cr.P.,C. is not necessary for prosecution under section 420 I. P,.C. It is only when sanction under Sec. 197 (1) is necessary that sanction should be obtained by the accused person who is actually engaged or is engaged in performance of official duties. The question whether sanction was required for prosecuting the appellant under section 199(1 ) of the Criminal Procedure Code before the appellant could be tried without any sanction under the section, is a matter relevant at the stage of sanction and not at the stages of sanction.

The appellant company was carrying on business in the erstwhile State of Travancore. In 1947, the Income tax Officer assessed the income of the appellant under section 3(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1949 50 and the respondent claimed that the income from the business profits could not be deducted from its profits made in British India or in an Indian State as the case may be. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the business was carried on by the appellant company within the meaning of section 24(1)(Per Bose, J., dissenting). Held, that the expression " income" in section 2(c) means a business in British Indian and not a business which is taxable in India. It is only when the profits of the business arise in what was British India in the case of the British India that the loss can be deducted but that is done under section 10 and not under section 24 (1)(per Sarkar, J.) The mere use of the words " loss of profits or gains" in the section does not justify the construction that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits and losses arising under the head business in an assessee company. The mere fact that the word " income " is not used does not support the interpretation that the words ' loss of profit or gains ' are sufficient to restrict its scope. The expression " loss" in s.2(c), means a loss which is not taxable in British territory and not taxable under section 12B.

The appellant company was a company carrying on business in Bombay region. The age of retirement was fixed at 60 and not 60. In the year 1959, the Company claimed that the age of superannuation should be fixed at sixty. The company contended that the trend in Bombay was to fix the age at 60. The Tribunal rejected the contention and held that the appellant had no power to reduce the age for which information was furnished by the various documents on this record. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal has not found that the industry in Bombay area was fixed as far back as 1950 while in the rest the age was fixed in later years. It is only in view of this finding that the Tribunal had found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay Region the trend had been to fix retirement age at sixty, and not at 55. [447 C] (ii) The award made by the Tribunal in the present case was not challenged before this Court. It was only in respect of the years 1958 and 1959 that the award was made at 60 or at 58. There is no indication at all as to how long ago the age should be determined. [427 G H] (iii) The trend in the Bombay region was to determine the age on which retirement age was extended to 58. It could not be said that the average of the relevant trend was to be taken into account by the High Court in some of its earlier decisions as to the relevant circumstances and that one of the important material considerations in this connection would be that the rate of retirement should be fix at 60, and that the norm for determining age of retire ment should be adopted at 60; and that it was not correct to say that the practice of the Tribunal was not followed. [547 C D] (iv) The approach adopted by the tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem is not very much acceptable. It has been pointed out that the High Courts had failed to notice the trend which the Tribunal has mentioned are, in many cases, the trends in Bombay and other regions to fix their age of superannua tion at 60 as 60.

The appellant company was incorporated in the State of Punjab. The Board of Directors of the company passed an order under section 237(b) of the Companies Act, 1913, authorising the Chairman to make an investigation and report thereon in respect of the affairs of the Company. The appellant filed a petition before the High Court challenging the legality of the said order on the ground that it was not maintainable as the Board had no power to appoint one or more persons as inspectors to investigate the affairs. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the company was being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members and other persons and that the appellant could not be prosecuted for fraud, misfeasance and other misconduct towards the company and its members. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Board was not empowered by section 237 to appoint a managing or other director as inspectors; (ii) the power conferred on the Central Government under section 235(1) read with section 10E(5), that the power to make investigation and delegated by it to the company Law Board is administrative, that the powers of the Chairman are judicial and not judicial. HELD : (i)(a) The power conferred upon the Central Govern ment by section 236(b), is subjective and that if the grounds are disclosed by the Board the Court can examine them for considering whether they are relevant. It may be mentioned that in paragraph 16 of the affidavit the Chairman also stated that there were circumstances suggesting that the business of the appellants was being managed with intent, to defraud their creditors, member or any other person. [322 B C] (b) The Board could not have delegated its function under section 236 to the Board but it had no authority to delegate it to itself. It could not therefore be said that the Board could delegate its function only in respect to the affairs and its member was not competent to make a report under section 9(1).

The appellants were tried and convicted for the same offence and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 1,000/ . On appeal by special leave it was contended that the circumstances under which the two sentences were imposed were not disclosed because dacoity as such was not challenged before this Court. HELD : (i) It is true that from each person a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market and the goods were found in their houses, there may be other elements which may point to the way as to how the presumption may be drawn. But it is difficult to think that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of to receivers of stolen property or could be placed in the custody of friends till such time as the original offenders could take them away. [723 B C] (ii) The circumstances under Which the two entries were made and the evidence on which the case of dacoity was established are those facts which connects him further with the crime. It is not necessary to state clearly in this case that within a short time, the presumption should be drawn from the facts found by the police. [700 C D] (iii) The fact that the accused were merely receivers of theft property from some other 20 persons or more. There may be cases where the stolen property was found in the house of many persons or several others who were the dacoits. It may be legitimate to think, that within short time the presumption is drawn. [623 G] (iv) The High Courts have been clearly drawn and in what circumstances the one presumption or the other may be draw from the evidence adduced by the prosecution. [750 C D].

The petitioners were manufacturers of 'thinner ' within the meaning of section 5(12) of the , and were granted licences for sale and sale of the same. The petitioners challenged the validity of the provisions of the Act on the ground that they had not been declared as poison for the purpose of restriction to be imposed on the posses sion for sale, and that the petitioners did not question the finding on any material. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Act was a Central enactment which is intended to regulate the import, possession and sale and the sale of poisons and the importation of the said goods was an offence under section 5 (12) read with section 5 of the . Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The Act is intended for regulating the import and disposal of any substance as poison in a rule made or notification issued under the Act. [222B] 2.1 The Act provides that no person shall sell or sell any poisons to any person without the previous sanction of the Central Government. If the Government thought in the circumstances that the possi sion or sale of such an article is to be regulated it could not be said that they have no power to regulate. [223C] 2:2 The Act does not contain a schedule in which the list of substances declared as poisons was listed. It is those substances which the Govern ment consider its possession for sale or sale to be regulat ed in the interest of health and safety of the society. It does not require that the same substance should be declared as an poison for purposes of the statute. [225D] 2(3) The Act has been amended by adding a schedule to the Act which is a schedule. The Schedule is intended only to regulate import, Possession and sale. It cannot be said to have any power to control the possession for the entire country. [226F G] 3. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity of the licence for sale. The object of the enactment is to regulate importation, possession or sale and not to make it obligatory upon the Government to declare any substance in a particular facts and situation prevailing in that area and the need to regu sion thereof desirable. If it thought in this case that the possess ment or sale was to be governed by the Act, then continued in force. [227F G; 228A] 4. The expression "poisons" mentioned in clause (x) of rule 2 is not a word 'poison ' and therefore cannot be understood as meaning any other thing done or omitted to be done. It may also be necessary that the said substance should he declared as 'poisons '. [228F G].

The assessee firm was carrying on business at Madras in drugs, chemicals and mercury. The assessee firm applied to the Tribunal for a supplementary statement of case on the question whether the debt of Rs. 2,68,385/ was not one incurred in the course of money lending business of the assessee. The Tribunal rejected the application but the High Court held that the debt was not a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the amount in question was not liable to be included in the taxable profits from business, profession or vocation where accounts were kept on the cash basis, if the debt is in respect of a loan made in the ordinary course of the business of assessee, and that the Tribunal had rightly rejected the claim. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the debts of Rs 2, 68,385 were not liable for the tax profits of the firm. [1039 C] (ii) The debt of the appellant other than money lending was not considered at all and the Tribunal disposed of the second part of the case by merely observing that it was an "accommodation" account to enable the Bombay firm to tide over the "financial crisis". The High Courts were right in treating the debt as a bad. [1139 C D] (iii) The expression "accommodities" in section 10(2)(xi) of the Income tax Act, 1922, is wide enough to include all debts which are due from the Bombay Firm and not from the Indian income. [1239 E] (iv) The Tribunal was right on the view that the amounts in question were not a "acc killings" within the meaning of section 10 (2)(xii). [1140 G] (v) The amount in dispute was not the 'accommodation ' account to be loans made in ordinary course. It is true that the expression "commodities", in section 2(xi) means "a sum which is due from a bank or money lender". In the present case, the debt in question had been paid by the assessee to the Bombay firms and the amount was not loans advanced in the normal course of business of their assessee.

The petitioners were owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 was passed in respect of the lands in question and the acquisition proceedings had lapsed. The petitioners filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the acquisition on the ground that they were not made within two years of the notification making the declaration under section 4 of the Act. The High Court allowed the writ petitions holding that since the awards in these cases have not been made within three years of notification making them, the entire acquisition proceedings could not be dismissed. Hence this Special Leave Petitions. Dismissing the special leave petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether the awards were made within the stipulated time is a matter for consideration and the suppresses material facts. [565F] 2. The award should have been made in two years from the date of publication of the declaration and that if no award is made within that period, the whole proceedings for acqui sition of the land shall lapse. [567A B] 3. The acquisition proceedings have lapsed. It is well settled in law that the relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court for such relief must come with clean and full disclosure of facts. If he fails to do so, and suppresses materials facts, his application is liable to be dismissed [565C D] 4. The writ petitions are liable to have been rejected on the grounds that the awards are not made in time. In view of the provisions contained in Section 11 A of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976, the award must be made within a period of two years. [568D E] 5. The Court should have directed status quo with regard to the possession of the acquired land in question in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the order of the High court.

The appellant, a non gazetted employee of the Bank, was appointed as an Assistant Manager in the Bank on January 1, 1959. He joined service with effect from January 1. 1961 and was confirmed in that post. The appellant challenged the validity of the award by a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the petition holding that the workmen would be fitted in the new scales of pay from January l, 1962 and not from January 31, 1959, and that the adjustment basic pay in the Sastry Award as modified by the Sastry award was not to exceed what point to point adjustment would give him or the maximum in the scale provided by the Desai award as modified. The High Court held that the appellant 's claim for increments under the Sastry awards was not justified. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The award of the Sastry Tribunal was not a mere executive order but a mere administrative order and it could not be said that the award was made in 1962. [902 F] (ii) The Award of the appellant did not contain any provision for revision of the Award as it was passed by the Labour Appellate Tribunal on January l 1959, which had been modified by placing him at the stage in the Award scale of pay as modified from January I, 1959 to February 1, 1962. The adjustment basic salary in the old scales was not the same as the provisions of the Desai Award as amended by the award as it stood prior to the date of the reference. [ 903 G H] (iii) The appellant 'rejected the claim for increment under the new Sastry Award on January I.A.I.R. 1958 S.C. 805 and the adjustment of basic pay was not in accordance with cl. (a) of cl. 100 as modified or the minimum of that scale or the actual basic pay as on January 31. 1. 1959, as modified, but for the modification of cl.(b) of el. (iv) the adjustment would be made on the basis of a revision of scales and not on the revised scales. [940 G H; 904 A] (iv)(a) The effect of the amendment in the award is that the additional pay in respect of the new scale was not only to change the basic pay but also to increase the basic salary as on 1st January 1959, in the scales then in force in the bank concerned. [943 B C] (v) The adjustment of the basic wages in the revised scale was neither a matter of any statutory or executive order nor was it a mere judicial order and could not therefore be said to have been made by the appellant in the present case.

The appellant, a resident of the State of West Bengal, was granted lease to the respondent No. 1 for a period of five years on the ground that he had been running a Five Star Hotel in Calcutta. The lease deed provided that the lessee would be entitled to construct a Five star hotel within the State and the remaining part thereof would be allotted to the appellant. The lessee filed an application before the Deputy Commissioner, West Bengal praying for a declaration that the grant of lease was void as it was not possible to renew the lease. The Deputy Commissioner rejected the application on the grounds that the lease deed was not in fact a part of the main Zoo hotel and was not a lease by the Government. The appellant filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority which dismissed the same. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended for the appellant that the interest and the requirements of the Zoo were totally ignored and not kept in mind when the decision was taken to lease the land to the Taj Group of Hotels. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The grant of a lease is a piece of evidence which has to be taken into account by the Govern ment in framing its policies and it is on a total evaluation of various considerations which have weighed with the Government in taking a particular action, that the court would have to decide whether the action of the Government was reasonable and in public interest. [263G H] 2. The purpose of the grant is to provide for the development of industries within the state. It is not necessary that the State should advertise and tell the people that it wants a particular industry to be set up within the Sate. If the State were giving effect to the policy, the Court would have been justified in proceeding on the basis that the land which was undoubtly Government land, to start with, was given to the Zoor logical Garden upon the terms set out in the two letters. [262A B] 3. The object of the state policy is to encourage setting up of industries for encouraging setting up industries within a State and invite those interested to come up with pro posals for the purpose. It would be difficult to say that the Government had not been able to advertise and ask the people to come out with proac tions for securing the highest price, subject, of course, to any other relevant overriding considerations of public interest, but in a case like this where the State is allo cating resources such as water, power raw materials etc. for the purposes of encouraging setting of industries, within the area, it would not be possible to contend that the construction of the provi sions of the land was not detrimental to public interest and that the purpose of granting lease was not bona fide. [267C D] 4. The State is bound to advertise the land in the open market and invite them to come within the purview of the Act.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1957 58. The assessee claimed that the amount of Rs.1 lakh paid by him in his favour and the gift of Rs,50,000 made in his name by his father was not correct. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the sum of Rs 1 lakh was wrongly included in the net wealth of the assessee. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee did not make valid gifts aggregating to Rs. 1,50 lakhs and that the gift was rightly included in its net wealth. In the reference under section 27(1) of the Act, the Tribunal referred to the High Court the question whether the assessee had made valid gift amounting to Rs, 1 lakh on the date of the gift. The High Court held that there was no valid gift and therefore the assessee could not be included in his net wealth as it was not permissible for him to make a gift of the value of the said amounts. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue: (1) that the Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide the question in the manner it did; (2) that there were no valid gifts and therefore, the assessee was entitled to claim deduction under section 10(1)(a) of Income Tax Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "any person" in section 2(g) of Act means any person who is not a banking company or which has no overdraft facility, by mere book entries even though there was acceptance of that gift by the donee would not effectuate a valid gift. [131D] 2.1 In the instant case, the High court had rightly held that section 10 did not apply to the gifts of Rs,. 1 lakh and Rs.50, 000 made by the deceased to his son and to his wife respectively. The question whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, it could be said that the income of the appellant was liable to be included under the property passing on the death of M. The Tribunal had rightly found that section10 did not come into play. [132E F] 2:2 In the present case, there was a valid gifts made by debit ing the assessee 's personal account in the books of the Hindu undivided Family with Rs. 50,000 and credited to the accounts of the deceased. The fact that the entries were made contemporane ously showed that the transaction was genuine and there was nothing to show that the interest which was paid by the donor would not be sufficient. [133G H] 3.1 The High court was in error in answering the question against the assessee, because it had held that Section 10 did apply to gifts of any value. It was held that it could not have been said that there had been a valid transfer of the amount gifted by the assessee to his daughter and to her wife respectively, and that this view was not open to him to raise an additional plea in the court. [134G H; 135A] 3:2 The High Courts were right in answering it in favour of the respondent assessee.

The appellant was appointed as Superintendent of Police in the Orissa State. He was posted as Superintendent and legal remembrance and member of the Orissa Service. The appellant challenged the order of transfer on various grounds, inter alia, that he had no authority to act as law secretary, superintendent and legal character Secretary to Government in the matter of appointment of a district judge from one post to another; that the High Court was not competent to recall them and that the orders of transfer were illegal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order was bad because it was passed by the High court without jurisdiction, and that it was not open to the High Courts to recall the orders passed by a subordinate court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) It is well settled that in a case of transfer from one cadre to another, the power given to the Governor is always exercised in consultation with the High 'Court and by and large on the recommendation of the High. Court, it is not open for the High courts to recall those orders passed under the Act as well as under article 235. [629 D] (2) The High Courts are within their powers in posting them as District Judges and not as District judges. They are within the power of the Governor and fall to be made by the State Government as part of the control vested in it by article 235, and they have the power to fill those posts by transfer of judicial officers already appointed or promoted and posted in the cadre must necessarily be outside the power. [625 E] (3) The power given under article 233 is not a power of superintendence over subordinate courts but only to make rules for the purpose of ensuring that the administration of justice is carried on by the executive, administrative or otherwise. It is not the function of the Court to interfere with the discretion of the executive authority in making the order.

The appellant, a vendor of the land in dispute, filed a suit for pre emption against the appellant and his brother 's son. The trial court decreed the suit holding that there was no infringement of Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the right of pre emptor to pre empted a right of preemption conferred on him by section 15(1) (b) and (vii) of Punjab Preemption Act, 1913 was not affected by Article 19 (1)(a) of Constitution; (ii) the expression 'other co sharers ' in clause 'Fourthly ' of Section 15( 1)(b) of that Act refers to only those co sharer who do not fail under clause 'Firstly ' or 'Thirdly ' and (iii) the appellant fell within the expression other co sharors ' in cl. (1) of section 15 (1). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The word 'other sharers" in clause (f) is wide enough to include a person who does not fail within clause 'fourthly '. [127B] 2. The expression 'any other co co shareer ' in Clause (f), includes a person whose share has been allotted to him or his son or daughter 's sons of the vendor or vendors. [128C] 3. The words 'other Co sharers who do neither fail under cl.(1), nor are 'thirdly ', 'fourth ' and 'fourth" of section15(1). They are not defined in clause 2(g) to mean 'any person who do no more than the co sharees ' jointly, only the other co share holders. [129D] 4. The meaning given by the two judge Bench on the expression "other co co co shares" in cl.(f) and 'Fourthally ' of section fifteen(1 ) is to be read as a residuary clause to ensure that no co sharee is left out. [131E F] 5. The language of the two Judge Bench is clear and unambiguous. It is clear from the context, it becomes clear that the legislature desired to confer the right on specified family members of the vendors or vendors in the first three clauses of section 14(1 (b). [132F G] 6. The object of the Court 's decision in Attam Prakash 's case was to deny the right to pre co shar er and to those relative or relatives of the vendee or vendors who were specified in the erstwhile first three clause of section 16(1 )(b), even if they happen to be co sharants. [132G] 7. The purpose of the court 's decisions is to give effect to the object of law, which is to protect the fundamental right guaranteed by Article 14 of the Constitu tion. [133A B] 8. The Court 'shall not interfere with the right conferred on a person by that provision. It may be open to the legislature to make an order for the purpose of giving effect to it. But in the instant case, the purport of the Act 's judgment in Attum Prakash ' case was only to deny that the right is acquired by specified family member of the purchaser or vendors and not the son.

The father of the appellants, who were the sons and the two sons of the first respondent, filed a suit for possession of the property on the ground that they had not been paid any consideration. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the sale deeds indicate that a sum of Rs. 1 lakh was received earlier and a net amount of Rs 1 lakh had been received later and that the appellants were entitled to get back the said properties. The first respondent filed an appeal before the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit for title and injunction was not maintainable as the appellants had not paid any amount of consideration and had no intention to accept the compromise. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The sale deeds are subsequent to 21.8.1987. The parties have signed the compromise deed which contains terms which they had accepted and all parties have accepted the document of compromise to be genuine. [541C] 2. The appellants were not entitled to any interest in the property prior to the compromise and it was open to them to make an application for permission to sell the entire property by 30th of April, 1991. [543D] 3. The suit for specific performance is maintainable as against the appellants. The alienees have no interest in property to part with the property which too has not been able to point out any justification as to why the compromise should not be acted upon and on the basis of it the litigation may not be disposed of. [540E] 4. The court cannot direct that the decree passed by the Court under Order 23, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the face of an objection of one of the parties to the consent of one or more of the alienees. [542F] 5. In view of the fact that there was a allegation of payment of Rs, 1 lakh to Sudarshan Gupta which is present in Court and counsel for the sons & after hearing the Advocate for the alienee, it cannot be disposed off. The High Court has rightly held that the compromise petition shall be accepted and in terms thereof the suit shall stand discharged and the alienors will have no liability to account for mesne profits.

The appellant company was a registered medical practitioner in Gujarat. The workmen of the appellant company were not entitled to the sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness. The Tribunal held that the benefit of sick leave granted by the Industrial Tribunal was admissible only in the cases of continuous illness and not on the ground of sickness, and that the claim for gratuity could not be examined by the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that (i) the benefits admissible under the Act in the matter of grant of sick Leave were such as to justify the rejection of the workman 's demand and the setting aside of the Tribunal 's award in that respect, and (ii) the benefit could not have been examined by it. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Industrial Tribunal had made an award for 7 days sick leave on full pay and dearness allowance in 1958, subject to the condition that the benefits would cease to apply when the benefits of the Act became available to the workmen. [84E] 2. The expression "any of the benefits provided by the Act" in section 49 of the Industrial Disputes Act does not deal with all aspects of the demand for sickness benefit and does not, at any rate, provide for the grant of leave on the full emoluments during the period of the employee 's physical incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his sickness. [85G H] 3. The award in the instant case was made effective from January 1, 1975, in the year 1958, and subject to condition that it would cease lo be entitled to receive any similar benefit admissible under section 49. [86A B] 4. The claim for 7 day days sick Leave on full wages is not a bar to the demand of the employees for sick leave. The question regarding the adequacy of the sick leave for which the sickness benefits were last paid, was not a matter of fact. [87C D] 5. The benefit of 7 days ' sick leave has been allowed to the workman of those companies. It is not necessary in the circumstances of the case to award the benefit under the provisions of the . [86G H; 86A B].

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the Bombay Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1950. The grounds were supplied to him on the ground that he had not been given a reasonable opportunity to make a representation against the order of detention. The appellant challenged the validity of the order on the grounds (i) that the grounds furnished in the grounds were vague and (ii) that it was not the want of bona fides on the part of the detaining authority, (iii) that there was no mala fide exercise of the power under article 22(6) of tile Constitution. Held, that the detention order must be quashed because it is not a mere pretence or pretence or merely an attempt to make out a case for interference with the constitutional right of the detenue for being afforded a proper opportunity of making a representation. The fact that the ground furnished in this case was vague or indefinite does not mean that the detaining authorities were not aware of the existence of any material on which the detention is based and the nature of activities imputed therein to the appellant. The power not to disclose facts, but to enable him to make an effective representation, cannot be implied in these circumstances. The right of detenue to be furnished particulars under article 21(6), which is a fundamental right guaranteed by article 22 (6) and the right of detained thereunder are subject to the limitation under article 19(1)(f). The power of detention can be exercised only when there is a clear allegation against the detenu that he has not been informed of the facts alleged. The mere fact that it is stated in the affidavit that the particulars mentioned in the ground were not vague or irrelevant, does not make the petitioner an opportunity to meet the allegations made against him.

The respondent was appointed as a member of the Indian Army Service in 1954. He was compulsorily retired from service on January 19, 1956. The Central Government ordered removal from service under r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954. On April 9, 1959, the Central Government directed removal from the service. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r.14 of the Defence Rules, 1955, was ultra vires the , and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. HELD : The words "subject to the provisions of the Act" in section 19(2) (a) are wide enough to include removal of a person from the serv ice of persons subject to the Act. [445 D] The words 'subject to such other provisions of this Act and the rules ', the Rules and regulations made thereunder, the central Government may dismiss or remove from the Service any person subject to this Act. Rule 14 is not ultra vires. It is a well settled rule that there can be no doubt that there should be rules and subject to such rules, the rules and regulations are subject to other provisions. The two sections must therefore be held to be ultra vires and void. [449 D] In the instant case, the respondent was compulsorily retire from service by a General Court Martial on January 20, 1956, and he was compulsorily compulsorily retired under r 14 of that Rules. Rule 15 is not inconsistent with section 19 of the , which provides for removal of an officer from the services. The rule does not require that rules and regulation made thereunder should be subject to any other provisions in the Act and such rules are ultra vires, and it is not necessary to make a rule providing for the removal from serv ice under r, 14.

The appellant company was carrying on business in the manufacture of tea. The Government of Bombay issued a notification under section 3(b) of the Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925, exempting the tea from octroi duty leviable under r. 21 of the Rules. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification by means of a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court held that the levy was not validly levied by the Panchayat as it had failed to fix the octroi limits in accordance with law. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Rule 3(a) of Bombay Municipal Corporation Rules, 1925 provides that the tax shall be levied from the date which shall be specified in the notice and he says that if the octroi duty has not been approved of by the time the resolution is passed, how could the tax be levied. The Municipality was entitled to object only to these two matters namely, (1) the tax or fee imposed and (2) the levy of octroi from April 1, 1963, was regularised. [222 B C] (ii) Rule 5(b), which authorises the levy is made by a Panchayat after considering the objections raised by the parties and giving its reasons for its decision, clearly shows that the rules prescribe the procedure for levying tax or fees and are not confined to octroi duty only. The Rules prescribe the mode of levy and are in no way inconsistent with the principles of natural justice on an assumption that the formalities contemplated by law were complied with. [223 E F] (iii) Rule 4(b)(i) provides that if a Panchayat finally decides to levy any tax or tax, it shall not be levied until the Government has passed a resolution approving the proposal together with the decision of the Collector before levying octroi. The rules prescribe procedure for imposing tax and are also provided in r. 5(a). [222 F G] (iv) Rule 6 provides that no tax shall have been imposed by the Government without giving the person concerned an opportunity to show cause against levy, and the period of sixty days of limitation commences from the publication of the notice under r, 4(i). The word 'may ' in r, 5(c)(ii) means the action taken under the Act and the rules. [225 F G; 222 A] (v) Rule 7 provides that a tax shall not have been levied from any date specified in r., 21 of these Rules unless it is otherwise provided by law. The rule does not prescribe the manner of levy or fee. It prescribes the procedure to be followed before the octroi can be levied and the rate at which it is levied.

The appellants were convicted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1). The appellants contended that the conciliation proceedings could be said to have concluded in the case when Louis Pereira was dismissed by the Chief Presidency Magistrate, Bombay and the proceedings went on till June 2, 1952. Held, that the settlement proceedings could not be said that the Conciliation Officer was bound to make his report within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceeding or within such shorter period fixed by the appropriate Government. The conciliation proceedings were pending at the time when Lhe appellant No. 1 was dismissed and the appellants were acquitted. The State of Bombay vs Maneklal, ; , followed. Held further that the provisions of section 12(6) of the Act are applicable to the case. The notice under section 12 (6) is given by the Conciliation officer within 14 day of the date of commencement of such proceedings or within the shorter period specified in section 20(2)(b). The conciliation proceeding could be continued only when the report was received by the Government and not before the Conciliation Officers. The provisions of the , are applicable only to cases where no settlement is reached, when the reports are received by an appropriate Government or when the proceedings are closed. The enquiry under section 20 (2) (b) is not a proceeding which can be said either within the words " pendency of conciliation proceedings" but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an end after 14 days but only terminate as provided in section 12.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the . The grounds of detention were served on him on the ground that he had been in jail and was likely to be enlarged on bail. He was informed that the said representation was rejected by the Government. In the writ petition filed before the High Court, it was contended that the order of preventive detention could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order was necessary for putting him back in jail. The High Court dismissed the writ Petition. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the order as contemplated by the Act and the materials on record. It is not necessary that the detenu should be released or that there was such a possibility of his being released or any other factors which can justify the detention of a person. [910C] 1.2 The grounds are not vague, but are vague and indefinite since such an order had no application to the facts of this case. [936D E] Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate, Burdwan & Anr., ; , referred to. In these circumstances it is difficult to hold that if a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of being released, the power of preventive Detention should not be exercised. [981F G] Rameshwar Fakir Hussain vs District Magis trate, Burdwan and Ors., ; ; Ramesh Yadav vs District magistrate, Etah & Anr. , ; Ramesh Singh vs State of Bihar & Ors., [1985] Supp.

The appellant, a manufacturer of gold and other goods, was granted license to the appellant for selling gold ornaments. The licence was renewed by the Administrator on the condition that the licensee should have regard to the policy and purpose of the Act in making his order. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 on the ground that it suffers from excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines had been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator was not unguided and uncanalised power without any guidelines for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. The High Court struck down the provision only on the grounds that it suffered from excessive delegating legislative power to the Administrator, but that is not decisive of the matter. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Administrator had no authority or authority to grant permission to carry on business as a dealer and that the section confers an arbitrary and uncanalalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to carrying on business in gold. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The objective of enacting sec. 28 of Gold Control was to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the ,and the scheme providing sufficient guidance to the administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. [955C] 1.2 In the instant case, the object and purpose for which the Administrator is required to exercise his power are to be gathered from the relevant perspective. The policy and the Scheme provide sufficient guidance for the Administrator in the matters of exercising the power of discretion conferred on him under sec. 5(1) of the . [956D] 1:3. In the absence of anything to the contrary, the Administrator can authorise the third person to carry out his directions. [936E] 1 :4. The Administrator is not empowered to refuse permission to grant or renew a license to a dealer. It does not impose any blanket or absolute prohibition upon a licensee from carrying on any business as money lender or banker on the security of any article, ornament or both unless authorised by the administrator. [951E] 2:1. The power conferred upon the administrator under secs. 5 (1) is subject to the restrictions imposed by the Act and the scheme giving effect to which it is made. It is not imposed by section 5(2).

The appellants were the owners of certain properties in Eragudi village. The lands were granted in Inam to the ancestor of the appellant 's father, who was the owner of the said properties. The respondents claimed that they had acquired title by adverse possession and that they were entitled to the possession of the properties. They also claimed that the appellants had acquired a title by way of adverse possession before the suit was filed. The trial court decreed the suit but the first appellate Court found that the lands belonged to the temple and that the respondents had been in management of the property. In appeal, the High Court held that the title of the alienees in regard to properties belonging to the appellant was adverse to the religious endowment from the very beginning, and that it was not open to the appellants to contend that they acquired title under adverse possession prior to 1st January 1929. The High Court also held that there was no evidence to show that the alienee had been removed from office by other persons who were in management. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit must fail because the transfer made by the manager of a temple in regard of properties belonging exclusively to the public was not valid and that if the title was transferred by the Manager, he could challenge the said transfer only after the death of the donor. HELD: (i) The question as to whether the alienation was effected by the appellant or by other person who had been appointed trustees or trustee has been removed is a mixed question of fact and law, and the High court was in error in reversing the decisions of the courts below by holding that the property belonged to a temple. [475 B] (ii) The suit must be dismissed as not maintainable because it is shown that the alienation made by a manager of the temple was without jurisdiction. It is open to doubt whether the decision could lead to the inference that if a part of the land is transferred by a Manager, the title to the property is adverse from the date of the transfer. [775 G] (iii) The High Courts were in error on the view that the question as regards the title must be decided on the facts found in the present case. It was not correct to say that the decision of the Privy Council was erroneous because the question whether a part was transferred or not was a mixed questions of fact, and law and the finding of the High Courts by the courts is perverse. [76775 B C] (iv) The contention that the transfer was for a valuable consideration must be negatived on the ground that it had been made on the basis that the transferor was in possession of some other person and not as an individual, and he dealt with the property as manager of his family cannot be accepted. [77775 E F] (v) The fact that the alienated properties belonged to one of the parties does not show that they are holding the same as managers of the trust. If that be so, there is no escape from the conclusion that more than 12 years have elapsed since the date when the transfer of the alienation took place, and so, if a suit was brought by respondents 1 to 3 on the date on which they were appointed trustees by respondent No. 2, it would not be correct to contend, that the transaction in question did not show the alienor had been taken over by other members who were acting as de facto managers of his properties.

The appellant firm was running a cinema theatre in the State of Jammu and Kashmir. The licence was renewed by the District Magistrate, Jammu (Jammu) on the same day. On April 27, 1979, the licensing authority granted the licence to the appellant firm for exhibition of cinematographs in the building known as Apsara Theatre. The appellant firm applied to the District Magis trate for renewal of the licence and the licence was cancelled by the Chief Justice. The District Magistrate rejected the application on the ground that the licence had been obtained by a person other than the licensee namely, Shri Ved Gupta who had been declared to be the sole licensee in respect of the Apsana Theatre. On appeal by the State Government, the High Court held that the renewal of licence could not be made in the name of any party other than his own. The High Court also held that there was no violation of principles of natural justice in as much as no notice or hearing had been given to the partnership firm before the order was passed. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the license for the Theatre was granted by the district Magistrate in the sole name of Ved Gupta and not by any other person other except his own name. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The licensing authority had no power under the Act or the Rules to make such an order. [578F] 2. The mere fact that the licensee was holding a licence in respect thereof did not amount to a license for a licence which entitled it to notice and hearing under the provisions of the Act before the licence is suspended, and since it is only the licensee who is held responsible under the law, he could be saved from any prosecution or other action under law in the capacity of licensee of the licensee. [577F] 3. The power to suspend a licence is conferred only by section 6 F of the , as one implicit in the larger power of revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the said Section are present, the licence has no jurisdiction to suspend the licence. [576G H] 4. The order passed by the Magistrate directing suspension of cinema shows in the Cinema premises that the cinema was being conducted by some persons other than those who were residing with him from outside the premises. It is not necessary for the licensing authorities to decide whether the licence in question was a license or not. [575F G] 5. The fact that there is no provision in the Act for suspension of the cinema shows that the licensing Authority had no jurisdiction under the . [576H; 577A] 6. The only reason stated by the High court for quashing the order passed against the appellant is that the said order was violative of the principles of Natural justice in that it was not possible to hold that the appellant was guilty of any offence or offences committed by others in the aforesaid premises. [574F G; 577B] 7. The writ petitioners were not entitled to be heard on merits and they should be given an opportunity to defend themselves before the licensing authori ty had passed orders under section 6 of the . The High Courts have held that since the licence of the Cinema was granted to the firm, it could not have been said that the licences in respect the Apara Theatre were granted by a competent authority. [580F G H] 8. The State Government has no power to cancel the licence under section 5 of the act which is an offence or breach of any law in force in the office of licensee. It cannot be said that there are two conditions of licence in the present case.

The appellants were the owners of certain properties in dispute. The appellants filed a suit for redemption of their lease on the ground that they had been granted by the Custodian under section 12 of the , and that they were not entitled to redeem them. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellants had no autho rity to issue any directions with reference thereto, and that the notice was invalid as it applied only to properties of the evacuee and not of the Custodian. On appeal by the appellants, the High Court held that section 12 applied only in cases where there was a lease and not by the evacuees but also by himself. The High Court further held that the respondents had no authority under section 10 to issue the notice in question under section 13 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that section 10 applied only when there was an order made by the evacuee under section 11 of the . Held, that the provisions of section 12 were not applicable to the present case and the notice issued under section 6 of the Bombay Act was invalid. The Custodian had the power to cancel a lease granted by himself and not on the Custodian himself, and he could not be said to have exercised any such power under section 9 to cancel the lease in favour of the appellant. Held further, that section 13 applied only where there is a lease, and not where there has been a lease. The provisions of sections 12 and 13 are similar to those contained in section 10 which confers power on the custodian to cancel an agreement with a person who had no right to do so.

The appellant was a minor son of Raghubir Singh. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order dated 6th August, 1977 passed by the Board of Revenue for Rajasthan and others. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had not filed an appeal under section 225 of the Act of 1955 and remanded the case to the Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, by his order dated 5th May, 1976. The Sub Divisional officer, Hanumagarh, in turn passed a fresh order on 6th September, 1976 directing that the ceiling area for Raghubir Singh may be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1956 and not according to new law i .e. in view of the fact that the Board had no power to make use of its powers of superintendence and control over all revenue courts. The appellant filed a revision application before the Board, which was dismissed by the High court on 6.8.1977. The Board of revenue, however, did not file an appeal against the order of the Sub Divi sioner. The respondent preferred a revision petition before the Revenue Appellate Authority and the Board by its order dated 14th April, 1975 allowed the same and set aside the order passed by him. In the writ petitions filed by the appellant before the High COurt, the High Curt held that the land in possession of Raghubir singh was ancestral. The State preferred an appeal to this Court against the said decision of the Board. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Board had by its earlier order dated 15th April 1975 directed that the Ceiling area for the appellant in law be determined as per old law and not by the new law. [726C] 1.2 The Board has by its own order dated 4th May 1976 directed that a ceiling area may be fixed according to existing law i,e. the Act. But sub section (2) made it clear that this superintendence would not be construed as giving to the High Courts any jurisdiction to question any judgment of any inferior court which was not otherwise subject to appeal or revision. [626D] 1:3 The Board having by its orders dated 5.5.1975 directed that if the ceiling is determined according with old law, it shall be deemed to have been done in accordance with old Law i. e.f. Act, 1955 and it did not apply to judicial proceedings. [625E F] 1 :4 In the instant case, the Board has passed a resolution on 5th April 1976 directing the ceiling of the land for the appel lant in law. The order dated 7th April. 1975 was confirmed by the Sub divisional Officer, who held that there was no provision for separate unit in Chapter III B of the Government of India Act, 1935 and that the applicant Raghubir Singh constituted one unit and not two units and the case was remanded to Sub Divisional Offi cer, Hanumant Singh. The sub Divisional Officer had by his orders dated 14.4.1975 ordered that the entire land in occupation of the appellant be determined on 5.6.1976. The appeal filed by him against the aforesaid order was dismissed. [613E F; 613A B] 2:1. The respondents having been aggrieved by the order, they preferred a writ peti tion before the Divisional Officer and the Revenue Tribunal.

The respondent, a newspaper published by the Ist respondent, was registered as an "newspaper" under the . The first respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act and the order made by the Central Government on the basis of recommendations of the Palekar Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the law reports were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the .
