In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the first respondent that the Act did not carry any news and that the public is not interested in them; that the provisions of the , which are being published by it were not newspaper as defined in the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law reports do not carry no meaning to say that the publication of the relevant provisions of a statute or notification should be construed strictly to make it a newspaper. [778C] 2. The expression "new ' has been used in the context of the statute and is in the nature of a penal provision which is enacted for improving the conditions of service of employees of the newspaper establishments and hence, even if it is possible to have two opinions on the construction of the provisions, they are not subject to any limitation. [781D] 3. The Act does not carry out any of the purposes of the legislation or the rules made thereunder. It is only when a statute has been passed that it can be said that the legislature has no power to enact it. [780E F] 4. The word "new" in section 2 (b) means "public news". The expression 'news paper ' as defined under section 2 of the Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955 is a beneficent legislation which is intended for the purpose of improving the condition of service. [779G] 5. The definition of "new souch" in the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1956, is a legislative practice which is to be construed as a whole and not a mere newspaper. It does not mean that the word 'new ' should be given its ordinary meaning. [783A B] 6.

The appellant was a licensee under the Bombay City. The agreement was executed between the respondent on the one hand and the appellant on the other. The appellant was described as an agent of the appellant. The licence was renewed for a period of five years from 1st of September, 1965 to 31st March, 1966. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for eviction on the ground that he was a tenant and also incidentally the question whether the Court of Small Causes, Bombay had jurisdiction to deal with the eviction petition in this case. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant was not a licensee and therefore, there was no estoppel against him. On appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the respondent was a lessee and not a sub tenant. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The agreement is a licence and not an agreement. [21E] 1.2 In view of the fact that the agreement was registered on the same day, it was clear that the licence was not put an end to by the appellants and that in any event by filing the application for eviction the appellant had granted an implied licence to the respondent licensee to continue in possession till a decree of eviction was passed in his favour. [22F] 1:3 The finding of the Small Causes Court that the Respondent was a sub lessee is wholly wrong and suffered from serious infirmities of law and fact and deserved to be set aside. [23G] 1.(4) In view Of the facts and circumstances of this case, it is a fit case for interference under Article 227 of the Constitution. [24F] 2. The High Court was right in holding that there was an agreement for leave and licence and the respondent had not been put an immediate possession of the premises on 1st February, 1973 under a subsisting agreement for licence. [25G] 3.

The appellant was a Ruler of the erstwhile State of Rajasthan. He was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, on the ground that he had been assessed to tax for the assessment year 1949 50 and the appellant claimed that the liability of the former Dholpur State did not fasten on the State of Ajmer as it existed on January 26, 1950. The appellant contended that the Ruler was entitled to the benefit of the new State of Jaipur under article 295(2) of the Constitution in respect of the obligations of the latter State of Dholpur to pay tax for that year and that the appellant had no right to claim the same. The High Court held that the agreement was not binding on the appellant as it emerged on January 25, 1950, and that it was a case where the Ruler did not acquire any rights in the property of the Ruler. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The agreement was valid and the State had no authority to create an estate or to impose any obligation upon the Ruler of Rajasthan under article 294(2). [179 E] (ii)The appellant could not be said to have been recognised by the new sovereign and reliance was placed on the continuance of laws in the covenanting State till such time as they were modified or altered. The agreement continued till they were repealed or altered, recognised that it would be binding on all the old States which then became subject to this that if the new state had not changed or altered by the existing State, it was liable in the same way as would have been the merging State if there was any liability on the merged State. [179 G H] (iii)The agreement continued until they were superseded or altered and there was no recognition of this liability by the old sovereign. The new State assumed liabilities of the old State and the new States became subject only to this, if there is any doubt about it that doubt in the present case the new Government assumed liability of its liability in the manner already referred to with respect to the liabilities of all old States. [180 G H; 180 A] (iv)The new sovereign was not a law and the same could not have been enforced in a court of law. The State of Bikaner had no power to impose an obligation on the Ruler to pay any tax or penalty for that period.

The appellant, a trader in cotton seeds, sold to the respondent for Rs. 1,000/ . The respondent purchased the goods from the respondent and paid the price of the goods at the rate of Rs. 2,000 per quintal. The respondent filed a suit against the respondent on the ground that the market committee had no jurisdiction to fix a higher rate than the market value of the commodity. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to deduct from the price or commodity in respect of commercial crops. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The respondent was not a trade allowance within the meaning of section 14 of the Act and therefore he could not be taxed under the Act. The question whether the allowance described as 'mahimai ' is a trade allowances depends upon the nature of that deduction. If it is a trading allowance, the said part of the bye law would be invalid as inconsistent with the provisions of section 19(1)(c) and (d). The respondent could not therefore be taxed on any transaction in respect Of commercial crops because he was not an 'trade allowance ' within the definition of section 2(g) of the , and that he was entitled to do so under the law. The fact that a market committee did not name the allowance or allowances taking them out of the pro hibition under section 14 would not affect the validity of that part of it. (ii)The respondent was a trade discount and the appellant could not claim deduction from the amount of the price.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to transportation for life. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts have not been justified in interfering with the sentences of death imposed by the High Court. [447 C] (ii) The sentence should be reduced to transportation in these two cases only because of the difference of opinion between the High Courts and the High court. There is no reason why the sentence should not be reduced, as there was no compelling reasons for departing from this practice in this case. [49 D E] (iii) The appellants were sentenced to life imprisonment on the opinion of the third Judge, without any justification. They were also convicted under sections 302 and 34 of Indian Penal code. There was no reason to depart from this course. [50 F G] (iv) The conviction of the appellants must be maintained. The sentence of death is set aside and the sentence of imprisonment reduced to life. [51 E] In the present case, the High 'Court had not considered the evidence of the eye witnesses as to the guilt of the accused but only on that of the two who did not give him any names it was clear that there was a difference in opinion in the High. The appellants could not be convicted under s 302 readwith section 34 I.P.C. [52 F G]. (v) The fact that the death sentence should have been reduced to imprisonment for life does not affect the discretion of the Court unless there are compelling reasons. There were no compelling reason why a sentence of murder should not he imposed unless there were compelling reasons, and in the absence of any compelling reasons it was impossible to depart therefrom from this rule.

The petitioner was appointed as Assistant Engineer in the Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India and was compulsorily retired by order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.76. He challenged the order before the High Court on the ground that he had attained the age of 50 years on 10.2.1972 and, therefore, on the date of his compulsory retirement he was reverted to the post of Assistant Engineer. The petitioner contended that he attained the 55 years of age on 10th February, 1972 and, consequently, on his attaining the age Of 55 years, he was promoted as officiating Executive Engineer in Class I service but on 4.9.1965 he was compulsorily retire from service with effectfrom 5.12.1972. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the petitioner attained the 58 years of superannuation on 10 2 1972 and therefore on the dates of his retirement he had completed the age at 55 years. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the order dated 4.8 .1965 was passed by a competent authority under Rule 56(j)(i) after he has attained the normal date of superannuation, and that the only question that fell for decision before this Court was whether a Government servant officiating in Class II or Class II service or post could be retired compulsorily by exercising the power under Rule 57(j). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The purpose of Fundamental Rules 56(J)(i), (j) and 8189 of 1981 are to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and the classification of Government servants into two categories covered by sub clauses (i) and (ii) has a purpose behind it. [690G] 2. The object of Fundamental Rule 56 is to confer powers on the Appropriate authority to compulsory retirement of Government servant, in the Public interest and, the classification is based on the opinion of the appropriate authori ty that the officer is in Class 11 or class II service. If he is only a temporary hand, he has no right to the said post and can always be reverted to his substantive post if any, on which he has a lien. [625B C] 3. The scope of Fundamental rules 56(1)(i)(i). The purpose for Fundamental Rules is to provide that Government servants in Class 1 or class 11 service or posts on substantive basis are outside the purview of sub clause (i). If the officer was not brought to an end by reverting the Government servant to his officiating post before the power of compul sory retirement is exercised, the Government Servant is in class I or class III service or a post on substantive, temporary or offi ciating basis. [613E F] 4. The language of Fundamental rule 56( j) is to give power to the appropriate authorities to compulsorily retired government servant in public interest. If the authority is not brought before an end, reverting the government servant to the substantive post before its expiry of his normal superannuation, it will be open to the Government to make a representation against such order and to consider such representation as may be considered by the appropriate au thority to pass orders on such representation. [566B C; G H] 5. The effect of Fundamental r 56(i)(ii) is that the authority should not have been deprived of the post and cannot be allowed to continue to hold the substantive posts or post at the relevant time and would come within the ambit of sub cl.(i). [666C D] 6. The benefit of Fundamental R Rules 56 (j)(1) is not available to Government servants, in Class l or class I service or category II service, or post on officiating basis. If it is only an ad hoc appointment, he is in a substantive capacity and he has entered into the service before attaining the normal superannuation age of 35 years. [646E F; G] 7.

The appellant Corporation was the owner of a bus owned by the respondent Corporation. The deceased died in the year 1963 and his wife died in 1964. The appellant Corporation filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,000/ as damages against the appellant Corporation on the ground that the said amount had been paid to the deceased. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the proposal was not accepted and as such there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation. In appeal by certificate, it was contended for the appellant that the policy of the deceased was a valid insurance policy and that the same was not a valid contract of insurance between the respondent and the corporation. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The plea that the deceased had accepted the proposal is not correct. It is true that the case set out in the plaint and the basis of the claim made in the notices sent to the Corporation was not that the proposals were accepted by the Corporation but it was also appropriated by it in its accounts and the said premium amount required for the proposal were not calculated. [357B] 2. The High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that there was a concluded contract of Insurance between the appellant and the Life Insurance Corporation and on that basis reversing the judgment and decision of the trial court. [358F] 3. The contention that the sanction was not given by the deceased, is without substance. It was also rejected by the High Court. [359G] 4. The mere fact that the premium was paid by the appellant did not alter the position as under the rules the payment of the premium could never amount to the acceptance of the proposal. [360F] 5. The case set up in the suit for damages is a pure question of law and it cannot be said that the plea that there is a concluded contracts between the parties, there was an concluded contract. There is no evidence that such a contract can be enforced by the corporation or its officers or agents. [361F] 6. The finding of the High court that there were no concluded contracts of insurance with the deceased did not amount to acceptance of proposal and as the policy was not considered, the terms of acceptance were not fixed and the premium amount needed for the proposed proposal was neither accepted nor paid. [362G H] 7. The fact that there had been assurance on behalf of the field officer and local agent to the appellant does not alter its position as per the rules. The defence taken by the State is that the contract of indemnity is complete by offer and acceptance. It cannot be disputed that the Corporation has accepted the offer and like other contracts, the contract is complete in all respects by offer. [363G H; 364A] 8.

The appellant, a company carrying on business in the manufacture of cotton and other textile mills, was granted a licence for manufacturing cotton and textile mills. The licence was renewed from time to time by the Government of India under section 109(a) of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939. The appellant filed an application before the High Court under article 133 (1)(c) of that Constitution for revocation of the licence. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the order granting interim injunction was a final order within the meaning of section 109 (a). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts had no jurisdiction to grant an interim injunction and that the appeal must be dismissed. HELD: (i) The expression "final order" in article 133(1)(b) is not a final one but a final decision on the rights of the parties in dispute in the suit or proceeding. [501 E] (ii) The word "final" in section 109 means an order which finally determines the points in dispute and brings the case to an end. It does not mean that the final order is final. [500 G H] (iii) The words "final orders" in cl. (a) are wide enough to include interlocutory orders. The expression 'final order ' in cl.(1)(a) means a final determination of the points and the finality attached thereto. It is not necessary that the decision on an issue put an end to the suit, or proceeding from which appeal has arisen, is not final. The word 'final ' in section 110(a), means a provisional order which ultimately determines the point in dispute. [525 B C] (iv) The question whether an interim order is a final adjudication by the Court of first instance does not arise because the decision upon the issue does not finally dispose of the dispute and the suit is not finally disposed of.

The appellant company was manufacturing cloth in the manufacture of cotton fabrics. The appellant company claimed that the assessable value of processed fabric would be the value of the grey cloth in its hands and not the value at which it would be selling the processed goods in the market, that the process adopted by the appellant was to get a declaration to the processor as to what would be their price at which he would be sold. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim on the ground that the cost of the processed fabric was Rs.5 and the manufacturing profit and expenses for the processing be Rs. 5 and then in such a case the value would be Rs,30, being the value thereof at which the processed fabrics were selling the finished goods. On appeal by the company, the Assistant Collector held that the price at the factory gate was not the assessable valuation of the process. The Revenue preferred an appeal to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The assessable value would he Rs.30, though the value is the value the value on the basis of the job work done is Rs.15 and the manufacturer so authorised agree to discharge all the liabilities under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. [345B] 1.2 In order to explain the position it is made clear by the following illustration: if the value in the hands of the assessee is Rs,20 and the value as deemed price at that time provided that the declaration as to the price on which he was selling the goods in that market would include only the price or deemed price. If the trader who entrusts cotton or made fabric to the controller for processing on job work basis, would give a declaration under section 6 of the Act and rules made therein, it is clear that the valuation at which such an assessee is selling the said goods and the person so authorised agrees to discharge the all liabiliities under this Act and Rules made thereunder, is the correct as sessable value. If, the trader, who entrust his cotton or makes fabric to him for processing, because those would be post manufacturing profits, he would have a declaration that the declared price at Which he would he selling the process in the factory that that would be done by the excise authorities as the assessable values of the manufac turing profit and expense. [346C D] 2.1 In orderto explain the situation it is necessary to include the trader 's profits who gets the fabrics processed, because these would be posts manufacturing profits. But if the trader whose entrusts Cotton or man made fabric is required relating to the prices at which his factory is selling that goods and, the person who so authorised agreed to discharge them all the legal liabilies under the aforesaid Act and these rules made thereon, it will be the correct that as sateable value is determined by the process of manufacture, the excise duty would be charged to the fabric on that basis provided that a declaration as regards the price of the processing would leave the processor 's factory plus his profit. [347D E] 2:2 In the instant case, the assessee company had claimed that it was entitled to claim that it should have been paid at the time when the goods were selling that the processed cloth was sold by the processor. The excise duty was charged on that price and the manufacture profit and expenditure for the process be Rs 5, then in the same case the price would be taken by the Excise authorities as its assessable value. [349F] 3:3 In order To explain the positions it is directed to include a manufacturer 's expenses, costs and charges plus profit, but it is not necessary to mention the trader"s profits which he gets the fabric processed, since those would have been post manufacturing profit.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on an ad hoc basis. He was confirmed in that post in the year 1974. The appellant was promoted as a Head Clerk on an Ad hoc basis and he was confirmed with effect from April 1, 1975. On March 14, 1975, he was promoted to the post of Head Clerk. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his absorption on a lower post. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was entitled to be absorbed in Government service as a head clerk on ad hoc ground. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for the purpose is not whether the appellant is entitled to he considered for promo tion or appointment but whether the Panchayat Samiti had the power to make appointments to the Panchayats. [738C] 1.2 In view of the deletion of section 33 of the Act by the Amending Act of 1973, the appellant could not have appointed him as a Sub Clerk on ad interim basis in January 1974. [ 739E F] 1:3 The appellant is appointed as Head Clerk in the Loharu Panchayat Samiti till he was absorbed in the Government service until he was absorption in Government Service. He is therefore entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the Panchayat Samities. [750G] 1 :4 The fact that the appel lant was promoted on an interim basis or in April 1975, or the further fact that he was appointed a Head clerk on April 1.1975 cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending Acts came into force. [751G] 2:1 The appellant 's appointment to the posts of Head Clerks is without authority of law, the Government was not bound to absorb him in the post as a Clerk. He could not therefore have appointed the appellant as a sub clerk on the date on which it purported to do so. [753B C] 2.2 The fact of the appellant being promoted as an ad interim measure or in May 1975 on a regular basis does not make any difference. It is true that the appointment of the appe lant to the Panchayat was made after July 13, 1974 when the amendment Act came into effect. There is no substance in this contention. [754G H] 2 :3 The right of being considered for promotions is a terms and condition precedent for promotion.

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to Math, Sauna or the deity Sri Thakur Gokarneshwar Mahadeoji. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Amauli properties were purchased by Mahant Shivshanker Yati from his predecessor in interest of the deity, and (ii) the property belonged to the Math or the temple as Mahant and therefore the claim to exemption from levy was made. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The fund from which the Amaikha is acquired constituted the personal property of the Math and therefore a claim to exempt from the levy was not made by the Sarbarakar of the temple. [662 D] 2. The property in question belonged to a Math or a deity and it was not known whether the properties were personal property belonging to the institution or the trust. It was not shown that the properties belonged to any Math or deity. The fact that the Amarendra Nath Banerjee, who executed the trust deed on November 12, 1892, bequeathing certain properties to the deity did not form part of the properties of the math or the idol. [663 D] 3. The income from the property was assessed to tax under section 4(1)(a) of the U.P. Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1948, as amended by the U P. Hindu Succession Act, 1950. [665 E] 4. The funds from which it was passed to Mahant Shivramik Yati were not part of any property belonging thereto. The properties were described by Mahant Ram Shankar Yati as properties of Math or temple. The appellant 's claim that the income from these properties belonged exclusively to the math and therefore, a claim for exemption from the payment was made by him. [664 E] 5. The trust was not accepted by the assessing authority and that the position in regard to those properties taken in the assessment proceedings was adopted by the Mahant only for the purpose of escaping personal liability to tax. [661 C] 6.

The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. They applied for a writ of certiorari to quash the order of allotment made by the Custodian General under section 12(1) of the , and the notification issued thereunder on March 24, 1955. The High Court dismissed their petition holding that the jurisdiction of the Custodian under section 19 of the Act was taken away by virtue of the provisions of sections 12(2) and 19 of that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that (1) the jurisdiction to revise the order had been taken away in view of the fact that subsequent to the issue of the notification under section 10 of the . The High court held that the power of the custodian under section 18 of the was taken over by the Central Government and therefore the notification could not be challenged. The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission invited applications from eligible candidates for the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Care and Development) in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (iterate) in the year 1985. The advertisement inviting applications from qualified candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was issued on June 8, 1985. On an application made by the State Public Service Com mission for re holding of the recruitment examination, the appellant State Public Services Commission decided to cancel the entire recruitment examination and asked for a fresh interview. The appellant State Government accepted the recommendation of the Commission and directed that the result of the written test be re hold in accordance with the rules. On receipt of the said letter, the Commission issued another advertisement inviting applica tion from eligible candidate for selection. The respondent State Public service Commission rejected the application on the ground that the appellant had better performance in the written examination and selected candidates securing lesser marks in the viva voce. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written examina tion and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the selection, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the appointment examination. [125E] 1.2 The situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a new interview of all eligible candidates on the basis of the viva examina tions and select those who on the date of the selection and select them, there were no justification to canceling the written parts of the recruit ment examination. There was no reason why the cancellation of the appellant 's written part could not be sustained. [126E F] 1:3 The situation can have been suitably met by set aside the selection. [127F G] 1.(4) In lieu thereof, the process of recruitment is to be completed within four months hence. There shall be no order as to costs.

The appellant filed a suit for recovery of possession of the Dera and properties attached to it. The appellant pleaded that the Dara was an independent Dera, and that he was in possession of his properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appeal had abated and that there was no ground for setting aside the abatement. The High Court held that after the death of the appellant the appellant was not entitled to recover possession of property of the respondent. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the appellant had no knowledge about the date of the death and held that the suit was barred by limitation. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The suit was for possession and management of the properties of Dera. It was in a representative capacity that the respondent was appointed as mahant of the Nera. The suit had been filed on the basis that the plaintiff as the lawfully appointed mahant was entitled to manage the properties. [490B] 1.2 In other cases of an assignment, creation or devolution of any interest during the pendency of a suit and the elected persons can be added as parties under Order 22, rule 10. The question whether the appellant has no knowledge regarding the date when the death took place when Shiam Dass was elected to be the Mahant of Dwara is not a matter of fact. [491C] 1:3. In other words, the suit is for possession, and management is a case of devolution of interest during pendency of the suit and its properties and it devolved upon shiam Dass by virtue of his election as mahantship in the Dwara after the demise of D.A. The fact that it was after Som Dass died that Shiam Das was elected as maafi, does not make any difference when we are dealing with the question whether a person has no title to the subject matter of the Suit. [493F G] 1 :4.

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State. They challenged the validity of the said order by filing a writ petition before the High Court, contending that the amendment of February 17, 1983 to the Fundamental Rules was violative of Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution inasmuch as it was made applicable only to those who had been compulsorily retired from 55 to 58 years. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the age of retirement was increased from 55 and not 58 to 58 by the Government of Andhra Pradesh by a notification dated October 29, 1979 and nothing had happened since then to justify reduction of the age. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the impugned order was violative Of Article 14 inasmuch as the power to reduce the age was conferred upon the Government by the proviso to article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitu tion. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The amendment of March 19, 1979 made in the Fundamental Rule is not violative of Articles 14 and 15 of the constitution. [419G] 2. The power to increase the age is a well recognised rule of law and it is well settled that the power conferred on the Government under Article 309 cannot be amended so as to confer arbitrary or unreasonable powers upon the executive authority to alter those conditions to their prejudice and in any event they can be amended by giving retrospective effect to the provisions contained in the Constitution. [420C D] 3. The object of the impugned amendment is to provide for a reasonable classification between persons who are similarly situated and those who have been granted such benefits as may be prescribed by law. It is not arbitrary or irrational that it is arbitrary or unjust in the circumstances of the case. [416D E] 4. The Government has acted arbitrarily without giving any opportunity to qualified and talented employees whose services were terminated by a notice dated October 30, 1979.

The Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973 was enacted to provide for the levy of tax on purchase of raw materials and other goods. The Haryana Sales tax Act, 1976 came into force from 9.4.1979. Section 9(1) of the Act provides that where a dealer liable to pay tax under this Act is not required to pay any tax under any other provision of this Act, there shall be levied subject to the provisions of section 17, a tax on the purchase of such goods at such rate as may be notified under section 15. The appellants were dealers in cement and steel products. They filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of section 9(2) of Haryana SalesTax Act, 1974. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions holding that the words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later on clause (b) of sub section (1) was deleted from the statute and that the said clause did not apply to the case where the goods were sold by a dealer and, therefore, they could not be taxed either under section 9 or section 24(3). The High court held that the expression "discharge of" in clause(a)(iii) later, clause (c) was inserted with retrospective effect from 27.5.1971. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the word "disposition" in cl.(b)(ii), earlier could not have been used in the context of section 5(3) and therefore the words 'or despatches the manufactured goods to a place outside the State in any manner otherwise than by way of sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce or in the territory of India within the meaning of sub s.(1) thereof, there should be no doubt that the effect of the decision is that the language used in cl. (a) and (b)(iii), later on, clause(b) was substituted by retrospective effect with retrospective operation from 27th5. 1971. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The words "or despatching the manufactured articles to a places outside the state" occurring in clause 2(ii) earlier, are not intended to include cases of despatches by a registered dealer for the purpose of export within the definition of 'turnover ' and therefore, the goods now in question were not exigible to tax either under s.9(1)(b) or section 6 or section 7 or section 8 or section 9. [351C D] 2. The expression "or despatch" in sub section 2(i) of section 4 of the Haryana Sales (Tax Act 1973, is a well known term used in section 5 of the Central Sales Tax and it has been used to include goods which are not covered by any other provisions of the said Act. [352D] 3. The word "sale" in section 9 (1)(a) means sale or despatch of goods to an place outside, the State or despatches of goods from any source in the State. It is a term "turnover" and it includes inter state sales. The definition of "turnover ' in section 2 (i) is not exhaustive but inclusive. [353D] 4. The meaning of the word 'sale ' is to be given its widest amplitude so as to include all transactions which are outside the purview of sub sections (1), (2) and 5(1). [352F G] 5. The term "sale", in section 3(i)(b)(iv) means a sale or despatching goods by a person who purchases them from any other source in any way otherwise than through the State, or despatch in the state of inter state trade or Commerce or in any other manner whatsoever. [354F] 6. The use of the expression 'sale" is not restricted to sales made in section 4(1), but only to sales effected by a Registered dealer for purposes of export outside the territory.

The appellant was a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1947. He sold the goods to the respondent who had purchased them from the respondent and delivered them to the appellant on board the ship and so no tax was realisable on these sales in view of the provisions of article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of the amount paid by him as tax under section 10(b). The trial court held that the goods were not liable to purchase tax under article 286 (1)(a) of tile Constitution and that the sales were exempted from tax under Article 286(i)(b). On appeal, the High Court held that there was no circumstance which would justify a conclusion that the parties came to a special agreement that though the sales had been made by some person who had given such certificate under section 8(b) only if the goods are not "despatched outside the State of Bombay" within the prescribed period, the exemption under article286 (1) (b) would come into operation. Held, that the words "the goods for the export" in article 286 were intended to be used in the sense that the property was intended to pass and did not include a transfer of title to the goods. The words "any person who has given such a certificate under s 8(a) are clear enough to cover the transfer of ownership of the goods and the purchasing dealer does not show to the satisfaction of the Collector that the sale had been despatched by him or by a person to whom he has sold the good.

The appellant, a married woman, was born in Bombay. She had been living with her husband and the respondent, who was a member of the family, and had also been living separately. The appellant 's father, who had been divorced from his wife, filed a complaint under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973 against the appellant for a monthly maintenance of Rs. 400/ . The Magistrate found that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance to the appellant. The Magistrate, after considering the evidence, passed an order under section 127(3) (b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, directing the appellant to pay monthly maintenance at the rate of Rs, 400/ per month for her husband. The High Court, in revision, reversed the order of the Magistrate and restored that of the trial court. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the courts below had failed to appreciate the true nature of the payment under any customary or personal law; (ii) the absence of mutual consent to live separately must be made out if the hurdle of section 125(4) is to be over come. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of eviction passed by the Magistrate under section 126(3)(b) is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the parties. [81 E] 2. Section 125(1) has compelling, compassionate and relevance in the context of section 127 and the benefit of doubt. The object of the Payment of mehar money is to avoid destitution of the divorcee and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. [82 F G] 3. The purpose of the paying mehar or ordained by custom has a reasonable relation to the object and is a capitalised substitute for the order under Section 125 not mathematically but fairly and section 127 (3) has great significance in the sense that the payment 'under any customary, or personal Law ' must be to obviate destitution. [83 E] 4. The expression "under any custom" in section 125 can operate to negate that claim. The legal sanctity of the payments is certified by the fulfilment of social obligation and not by a ritual exercise rooted in custom. If the first payment by way of mear or ordaining by custom is not a mere formality, it must be held that the object of payment ' under any custom is to obviate the destitution and to give her with the wherew incite to maintain itself. [84 E F] 5. The principle of "underany customary or Personal law" must be applied to the facts of each case. If any in statutory interpretation belongs to the ill used wife and the de facto payment is not to avoid disharmony, the marriage cannot be held to be void. [85 G H] 6. The intention of the legislature is that no husband can claim under section127(3), absolution from this obligation under section 5 towards a divorced wife except on proof of payment of a sum stipulated by customary or Hindu law. [86 E F; 86 A B] 7. The distinction between a decree for maintenance and a decree passed in a suit for maintenance is manifestlyto avoid despture, destitution or to provide the order u/s 125(3). The principle that no wife can claim u/S 127(1)(b), absense from this liability under section 488 cannot operate to defeat that right. [87 E F G; 86 C] 8. The law is that a husband can get an allowance for maintenance only on proof that he has been divorced by her husband except on proved of payment. The quantum of maintenance is certified in the prescribed form and it is not necessary that the husband should be given any benefit of a decree. [88 E F, 86 A] 9.

The appellant was a public limited company. The appellant was the highest bidder for Rs.11,900. The bid of the appellant was accepted by the Collector and he was given the shop of the respondent. The order was passed pursuant to the order of the Collector. The Collector issued notice under section 6(1) of the Bihar Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1972 calling upon the appellant to show cause why he should not be placed in the black list for future under the orders passed by the Collec tor. The respondent challenged the said notice before the Collector on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The order of Collector is set aside and the appellant is directed to be placed at liberty to pass any order in accordance with law. [868G] 1.2 In the instant case, that portion of the order directing that the appellant be placed under the black List for future contracts under the Collector is setting aside. So far as the cancellation of the bid of appellant is concerned, it was an implied principle of natural justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. [ 869A B] 1:3 The last portion of order directing the appellant not to be heard and make representations against this order. In that view of the matter, the last portion in the order in so far as it directs black listing of the appel lant in respect of future contracts cannot be sustained in law. In the premises that portion is not affected. [873B] 1 4.

The appellant, a tenant of a building in the city of Madras, was allotted to the respondent. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground that the premises leased under exhibit P 1 had also been conveyed to the appellant and that the appellant had no right to recover the rent from him. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the building on the land leased under the exhibit P1 had also not been conveyed by the respondent to the appellants, but only a vacant site, and that it was open for the tenants to seek fixation of fair rent in respect thereof. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court which dismissed the same. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that since the subject matter of the lease under exhibit PW 1 had been conveyed only to the Corporation and that there was no relationship of landlord and a tenant, the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to determine the fair rent. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The question whether the appellant is a tenant in or landlord of the building as claimed or not depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. [553B] In an application under section 4, the jurisdiction of the Rent Control ler has to decide the question as to whether the landlord is a 'tenant ' within the meaning of section 64 C.P.C. The Court has to determine whether the tenant is a "tenant" or not. If the relationship exists between the parties, the rent controller must proceed with this incidentally but this is not one of direct issues before the Rent Tribunal. [554D] In the instant case, the question on which the jurisdiction was excluded from the purview of the civil court 's jurisdiction as well as the provisions of the Act, the Court has no jurisdiction in the matter. The question on the other hand is whether the order of the Court of Small Causes in the earlier rent control proceedings deciding to the contrary and fixing the fair rents of item 17 (2) is a final decision under section 64C which cannot be questioned in appeal to the Court. [555F G] In view of this finding, it has to be in the negative. [557H; 556A] The question as regards the applicability of the provisions contained in section 4 of the Bombay Rent Control Act, 1958 is only a determination as to the fair and standard rent for the premises.

The petitioner, a member of the Mysore State in which he was given a provisional seniority list on an integrated seniority list, was still to be prepared after hearing objections. The petitioner challenged the validity of the final list by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court held that the petitioner had been wrongly denied relief against the final inter State seniority list although he was not heard and therefore could not be heard by this Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the principle recognised in Shankariah 's case (supra) was applicable to such a case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The principle recognised by the Supreme Court is that a person whose seniority is to be determined under section 115 of the Act must be given. If he was to have that opportunity, it cannot possibly be said that he should have a further opportunity to object to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list. [828 E] 2. The principles recognised in the decision of this Court are not applicable to a case where the final lists on an inter State basis were prepared contrary to the rules applicable or is vitiated on some ground showing that a condition precedent to the finalisation of the list was absent, it would still be inviolable and unnecessary for determining whether a particular procedure should be adopted for determining the seniority. [829 E] 3. The decision of the authorities concerned will have to stand.

The petitioners in both these writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of iron and steel items. The petitioners in the writ petition challenged the validity of sub para (10) of para 218 of the Import & Export Policy 1978 79 as well as the Export House Rates Control Order, 1985 on the ground that the said licence had been granted to the petitioners under the Import and Export Policy for the period 1978 79 excluding those items which were banner in the policy for the year 1978 79. The writ petitions were dismissed by this Court. In the appeals before this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that sub para(10)of para 218 which lays down that Additional licences issued to Export Houses/Trading Houses prior to April 1, 1988 would not be eligible for the flexibilities in the import of items of raw materials, components and consumables covered by Appendices 3 and Part A, and items of non OGL capital goods (other than those covered by appendices 1 and 2 were also entitled to a similar relaxation. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The licences issued under the Export Houses and Exports (Control) Act, 1978 79 are valid for a period of 12 months and the said period has expired during the pendency of these writ Petitions. [236B] 2. Under the Import Policy 197879 the basis for grant of Additional Licences is the minimum quantity of raw material which can be imported under the prevailing Import Policy. The import policy is to be given on the basis of not foreign exchange earnings from the exports actually made and the value of such additional licence is only 10% of the net foreign exchange earning. [237C D] 3. Under para 218(10), the Additional licences are to be granted on the strength of notforeign exchange earnings for the years 1978 79 and 1979 90. The Additional Licences are to he treated at par with Export Houses who have been granted Additional licences on or after April 1. 1988 in as much as the conditions of eligibility for grant or additional licence are fulfilled. [238D] 4. Under paragraph 218(11) of the Policy 1978 80, the basis is for grant and not for an extra period under the import policy. The Export Houses have been given on a basis of their exports made during the period 1977 78 to 1978 79 in accordance with the Import policy. It has been contended that under para 218 (10), Additional licences were to be issued on the date of exportation of the goods and not on the dates of export. [239D] 5. The additional licence granted to Export House/Trade Houses/Grading Houses/Fixation of Export Houses is the f.o.b. value of the exports made in 1977 78 and the Export Policy 1979 79. It is, therefore, directed that the period of validity of the Additional Licences should be extended so that the petitioners can avail the same and are able to import the goods which can he so imported under this country. [240E F] 6. The period of renewal of the additional licences under the Customs & Export policy 1978 79 has been fixed by the Import Control Policy 1978 1979 79 and it cannot be said that the Petitioners who have not been granted additional licences on the grounds of policy of canalisation of imports under sub para.(10) are entitled to an extra benefit. [241F] 7. The licence issued to the petitioner is valid for the periods of validity. [242G] 8. Under Para 218(1), the petitioners are entitled only to a certain amount which is more than Rs. 10 lakhs in the year 1987 88 and in subsequent years and obtaining Additional licences for a lesser value under the said policy. [243F] 9. The petitioner in the instant case has been granted an additional licence on the footing that the Additional Licence issued to them was valid for one year and the same period has lapsed during the pend ing of these Writ Petitions.

The appellant assessee, a manufacturer of certain goods, was manufacturing the said goods. The value of the drums was determined at the time of removal from the factory in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer. The appellant claimed that the cost of packing could be included in the assessable value only when the packing is either manufactured by the assessee or is purchased by the assesses. The Assistant Collector held that at the relevant time, the cost was not includible in the taxable value, but only a part thereof, and rejected the claim on the ground that the packing was not returnable to the buyer, and that the price of packing contemplated in section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act was not the cost incurred by the manufacturer or the supplier. The Appellate Assistant Collector upheld the order of the Assistant Collector. In appeal, the Tribunal held that the value of packing would be included under the assessable valuation only when packing is neither manufactured by assessee nor is purchased in the course of removal in packed conditions and the container were not returned to the buyers except where the packing has been of durable nature and is returnable by buyer to the assessee. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that since at the date of removal, goods were delivered from the premises in packed Condition and the packing were not served by the seller, there fore, the value had to be included as determined and section 4 (4)(a) of Act, and therefore, the price for packing could not be included. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The cost of the packing envisaged in section4(d)(ii) is repugnant to the very scheme of section 4. [995B] 1.2 In cases where the Act provides for excise duty with reference to value of excisable goods, while determining the value, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is integral part of the cost and is payable by the dealer, in all other cases the cost or cost of such packing would have to be excluded in the assessment under section 4.(4)(b) of that Act. [996C D] 1:3 The object and purpose of the levy, the meaning of the expression 'assessable value ' as interpreted in section 2(ii) of Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944, is to provide for the levy of excise duty on excisable goods. It may be necessary in this connection to refer to the observations of this Court in Union of India vs Godfrey Phillips, by the learned Attorney General. If the manufacturer supplies the drums and charges the customers separately, then under section 5(4) (d)(1), the cost is to be added to the price except where packing is of a durable character and is determined by the buyers to the manufacturer. [997G H; 998A] 1 :4. The cost for packing envisaged by section 4 of the Central Excises and Salt Act is not the value.

The appellant was convicted under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for 15 months under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (1)(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The conviction was confirmed by the High Court in appeal. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand and had also received the amount on 22.10.1975 itself passed orders and closed the file relating to show cause notice. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The prosecution case is not supported by any evidence. It is true that the conviction under section 165 I. P.C., and section 5 of the Act is to be maintained no separate sentence need be awarded under section 4(1) of Prevention of Corpo ration Act. [337B] 2. The appellant had a consistent case with the transaction of loan or return of money by PW 1, the recovery of the currency notes from the appellant was not challenged. The evidence of PW 1 is insufficient to hold that the appellant had been guilty. It must further be shown that the explanation offered by the appellant is probable and there is no conclusive evidence to hold the appellant guilty conduct of the appel lant in view of the presumption arising under section4(1). [338C D] 3. The burden resting on the accused person in such a case would not be as light as it is where a presumption is raised under section 114 of Evidence Act and cannot be held to be discharged merely by reason of the fact that the Explanation offered by him was reasonable and probable. It should further be proved that the accused had received a sum of money which was not due to him as a legal remuneration. [340D] 4. The presumption created by the provision cannot be said to be rebutted. The explanation given by the accused is sufficient to be accepted. The onus resting on him is also not impressive. [341E F] Dhanvantrai Desai vs State of Maharashtra, AIR 1964 SC 575; Dhanvantraj Balwantrai Desai & Anr. vs State, AIR 1965 SC 575 and Dhanvantaraj Balwantraiji Desai vs state of Maharashtra & Ors., AIR 1966 SC 575 referred to.

The appellant company was a public limited company. The respondent company was incorporated in the State of Bombay and its registered office at Bombay. In the year 1973, the respondent company made an application under section 630(1) of the Act for permission to carry out certain repairs and repairs. The Company filed a complaint against the appellant company alleging that the respondent had committed breach of contract with the company and that the company was guilty of wilful withholding of property in respect of which the company had been appointed as its director. The Magistrate, after recording evidence, held that the appellant was guilty and ordered the company to pay Rs. 1,000/ . Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The words 'all such property" used in section 631 are wide enough to include not only a property of the company but even a part of it which is owned by a company. [176E] 2. Section 631(l) does not require that an officer or employee of the Company should be given a reasonable opportunity to explain his conduct. Therefore, the words "any other property" occurring in sub sections (l) and(b) must be construed to mean only a part or whole of it. [181A B] 6. The language of section 631 is clear and unambiguous and there can be no doubt that the word 'office ' has not been defined by the legislature with the object of providing a summary procedure for retrieving the property of company and the duration of such right would be co terminus with the terms of employment and the right would stand extinguished with the termination to the employment giving rise to an obligation to hand over the property back to the company, and that is why the expression "office" has been given in sub Section (1). The appellant, a public religious trust, was the founder of the temple. The deity installed in the temple was dedicated to the public and the appellant was appointed as a private trustee. The appellant 's father died in 1951. In his lifetime he had been succeeded by Guru Govindbuwa and the latter by his son. The respondent filed a suit for declaration that the Sansthan was a private property and not a public trust. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the temple is a private temple and it was also transferred to the appellant 'Saints in favour of the deity. In appeal, the High Court held that the properties were private property, but the High court reversed the decision of the Charity Commissioner by his order of October 16, 1959 and declared the Sansthan to be a private trust. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the endowment was a public temple within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act and therefore the property was not a private or public religious endowment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The dedication to the temple by the founder is not a mere religious trust but a public charitable institution. [526 B] (2) The endowment was in favour by Guru who was maintaining a temple and the offerings were made with the object of maintenance of the worship of the idol. [525 C D] (3) The High Court was right in holding that it was not open to the respondent to prove that the property is a public institution. When the origin of an endowment is obscure and no direct oral evidence is available, the court will have to resolve the controversy about the character of the trust on documentary evidence if any, the object and purpose for which the trust was created, the consistent manner in which the property has been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the manner inwhich the property had been dealt, or managed. [500 E G] (4) The temple is not private or a public endowment within the definition of section 3(2) of Act. It is clear from the language used in the document that the deity installed therein was intended by the Founder to be continually worshipped by an indeterminate multitude of the Hindu public. [511 E] (5) The trust was a religious endowment within its meaning and it could not be said that the trust is a Public religious endowment, as the persons who were entitled to worship at the shrine of the appellant or the Sansthan for the purpose of maintenance thereof, the nature of devolution of the property, are all important elements in determination of the question whether a property is private or an public religious endowments. [506 G H] (6) The evidence of the founder and the founder clearly showed that the appellant installed in his temple was intended to be continued as a public deity. The dedication was made with a view to maintain the temple and for the purposes of maintenance, of the public, to all intents and purpose as a matter of right without the least interference or restriction from the temple authorities to foster maintenance of worship of worship. [628 G H; 506 A] (7) The appellant had been rightly held not entitled to claim that the suit was a 'private property ' within the scope of section2(13). [527 B C] (8) The question whether the property in question was a "public trust" is a pure question of fact. It may be a mixed question of law and fact depending on the particular history. Whether a property was a Public temple or not depends upon the particular facts and circumstances of each case.

The appellant was arrested and detained under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876. The appellant challenged his arrest on the ground that section 46(2) of the Act was violative of article 21 of the Constitution inasmuch as it contravened article 14 of the constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that section 16 of the said Act violated article 21 and article 14. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 46(1) of Bombay City land Revenue Act provides for two different and alternative methods of recovery of arrears of land revenue. It is not necessary that all the provisions of all the State laws are, mutatis mutandis, to be read into section 46 (2). The expression "any other law" in article 21 means a territorial classification which is based on an intelligible differentia and the subjection, for the purpose of the recovery of tax demand from defaulters of each State. [157 D E] (ii) Section 16(1), as it then stood, provides that the Collector shall proceed to recover the certified amount as if it were an arrear of land Revenue. The expression 'any other person ' in article 14 means a person who is not liable to pay up the Union demand and is entitled to recover from him the amount specified therein as if the same were an arrears of Land revenue. [158 E] In the present case, the appellant had been arrested and was detained in jail for a longer period of time. The State laws provide for two distinct and alternative modes of recovery. The object of the section is to provide for the detention of all defaulters who may not pay up their demand. [159 G H] (iii) Section 17(2), which provides that no person shall be liable to any penalty under section 16(2). It is only when in the matter of recovery, the amount payable is paid as an arrear or revenue and it can be done easily by suitably amending section 46. The word 'any ' has been defined in the Act and yet the word 'may ' has not been defined. [160 G H; 157 A] (iv) Section 13(1)(a) provides for three different modes of recovering the amount due from defaulter to the same coercive process devised by their own State, on a consideration of local needs, for recovery of the dues of each of such classes of defaulters to the said amount.

The respondents were the employees of the Port Trust, who were employed in the Port of Bombay. The respondents were paid overtime wages for the period from 1st April, 1963 to 9th March, 1964. They claimed that they should be paid overtime at the rate of Rs. 10 per day and that they would be entitled to three hours ' overtime. The Tribunal held that the shore crew at the bottom of the work in a week was 48 hours per day for six hours and that there should be a fixed number of hours of rest in the work day. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The provisions of section 13 fixing the number of days of work in the ordinary working day are not applicable to the present case. [860 B] (ii) The Act and the Rules do not contemplate that the interval for rest shall break up the hours of work. It is for this reason that a variable recess is in force at the Prince 's and Victoria Docks and due. [861 C] (iii) The definition of " hour of work" in section 13(1) which says that the maximum number of times of work should be fixed under this Act by the hour, by the day or by such a longer wage period as may be prescribed, works on any day in excess of the number and for any work in excess thereof. [862 E] (iv) The term " hours of working" is not defined at the same time but at the place where the workman is either made to work or the interval is not specified. The definition does not mean that the period of work must be fixed on a particular day. It cannot be said that the Act and Rules are intended to regulate the inclusion of an hour of rest.

The respondent was a thika tenant of the Thika Tenancy Act, 1949. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for ejectment on the ground that he had been in possession of the premises and that he was not liable to ejectment in view of section 3 of the Act as amended by the West Bengal Thika Tenants (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952. The trial court held that the appellant had failed to prove his case and dismissed the suit. In appeal the High Court confirmed the decree. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was not entitled to the benefit of the Calcutta Thika tenancy in view Of section 3(2) of the West Bena Tenancy Act 1949 as amended, and that the definition of a thikka tenant in that Act was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. HELD: The provisions of the Bengal Thikka Tenancy (Amendment), Ordinance 1952 were prospective only. Section 4 provided for the procedure for ejectment of a tika tenant in respect of certain premises. The section provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, a thita tenant shall be liable to eviction from his holding on one or more of the specified grounds and not otherwise. Section 5 provided that if at any time between the commencement of the said Act and of this Act, the landlord was required to consider whether any of the grounds mentioned in section 3 were available to him and if so, he did not have to file a suit but apply to the Controller for an order in that behalf. The provisions contained in the Bengal Tenancy Act were prospective and as such inapplicable to the case. [1055 H; 1056 A B] The words "any of the ground specified in section 4 in sub section (2) are wide enough to include any other ground which may be taken in the notice under section 4. The legislature has not intended that the provisions of a particular Act should apply to all suits, appeals and proceedings pending on 21st October before any court or before a person deciding an appeal under section 27 of the .

The appellants are working as Senior Assistant Engineers in the pay scale of Rs.500 1,000. They were appointed as Junior Assistants on a regular basis and they were given the same scale of pay. The High Court directed that all the posts of Senior Assistants be placed above the cadre of Senior Assistant Engineer. The State Government issued a circular dated July 2, 1976 laying down the criteria for entitlement to higher pay scale. The appellants challenged the validity of the circular on the ground that it would be violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The learned Single Judge allowed the writ petition and directed that the appellants should be given the benefit of higher pay scales which is being given to Superintendents or the Section Officers. The Division Bench also held that the classification made by the State Government was not based on seniority alone but on the basis of seniority alone, but on a rational nexus with the object to be sought for, as reiterated before a certain amount of value judgment by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the circular did not accept the claim of Bench Secretaries for giving them pay scale equal to Section Officers or Private Secretaries and that the Circular did not give them pay scales equal to section officers or private Secretaries. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The principle of "equal pay for equal work" has to be construed in the first place. [292B] 2.1 The principle is applicable to grant of higher scale of Pay and that merit will be evaluated by a competent authority. The classification made under the Rules, therefore cannot be said to be violative Of Article 14. [293C D] 1.2 The High Courts have completely overlooked the criterion provided under the rules. The rules thus make a proper classification for the purpose of entitlement to lower pay scale and other conditions of service. If it has a rational relation with the objects to be asked for, the classification is not on the same footing as that of section officers who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other condition of service.[292D] 2:2 The principle laid down by this Court in State of U.P. vs Dr. Ram Kumar Gupta & Ors., [1985] 1 SCR 891 is not applicable to the instant case because the principle of equal pay for Equal work has to he construed in first place, and it cannot be interfered with by the Court unless it is demonstrated that either it is irrational or based on no basis or arrived mala fide either in law or in fact. [294D E] 3. The principles of " equal pay" have to be read in the second place. If the principle is applied, a rational relationship with the purpose to be seeking for, and to meet the ends of justice would be defeated by the court unless it was demonstrated that both it is arbitrary or based upon no basis nor arrived at mala fide. [295E] 4. The doctrine of "equ pay for equality" has been evolved in the case of equality before law and equal protection of Article 16. If there are two different groups of employees, one cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgments by those who are being charged with administration in fixation of the scales. [296F] 5. The Court has completely overlooked this criterion provided for equal pay to Section officers or Private Secretary of State Government. The rule thus makes a proper distinction between the two groups of posts with different pay scale, and that seniority will be determined by a duly constituted authority. [297G H; 298A] 6. The concept of " equality" is not an abstract doctrine of equality but an equitable principle of equality. It is not possible to say that there should be equal pay in the same cadre of persons performing the same or similar work or duties.

The appellant State Government issued a notification under section 127A of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961, authorising the State Government to levy property tax on lands and buildings. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification by filing writ petitions in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the impugned notification was invalid as it purported to have come into force with effect from April 1, 1976 when clause (d) was inserted in section 127 A of the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that respondent 1 had waived its right to levy tax under section 129A of that Act and that the notification was bad as it was issued after the enactment of section 69(d). Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The property tax is imposed by respondent 1 under section 128A of a Municipal Corporation Act. Section 127A provides for the constitution of special areas and as from the date the Special Area Development Authority has power to impose the property tax. [682C] In the instant case, the property taxes are levied by respondent No. 1 under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957. The property taxes is imposed on lands, buildings and buildings and not on buildings. It is a well settled principle of construction that where a statute creates a new area or a new one, it must be construed as a whole and not in any manner defeated by the legitimate exercise of taxing power under section 69 (d). [683E F] The State Legislature has no competence to pass a law on the subject and the State Legislature had no competence. It was therefore competent to pass the impugned Act by reason of Entry 52, List I read with Entry 24, List II.

The appellant, a tenant of certain lands in the State of Andhra Pradesh, was granted subsequent to July 1, 1945, by the Government under section 3(1) of the Abolition Act. The appellant contended that the lease was for a period exceeding one year and not for a further period than one year, and that as the lease had been for a continuous period of one year it was not enforceable against the Government. Held, that the words "such rights" in section 3 (1) are wide enough to include rights created after July 1 , 1945, and the right conferred by the second proviso is not restricted to those rights created before the notified date but only to those specified rights created prior to July I, 1946. The words " such rights" used in section 2(2) of Act 1 of 1945, are wide and do not include rights acquired after July I , 1946, and therefore the Government was competent to exercise the right under the second Proviso. Held further, that it is well settled that the word "such right" in the third proviso must be read as meaning a right created before July 1. The first proviso does not apply to the present case because the words 'such rights ' are only voidable at the instance of the Government and not by the State. The second proviso applies only to rights created on or after July l, 1945. The effect of the second provisos is that all rights created subsequent to the date of the notification shall be deemed to have been valid and enforceable both by and against the Govern ment by the operation of the body of sub section (1).
